0.title: Do Not Be Shaken
0.overview:
Second Thessalonians was written from Corinth only weeks or months after the first letter — probably in the autumn of AD 51. Paul had received further news from Thessalonica, and it was concerning. Someone — perhaps a forged letter, perhaps a claimed prophecy — had convinced some in the congregation that 'the day of the Lord has already come' (2:2). The eschatological excitement of the first letter had curdled into eschatological anxiety, and in that anxiety some had stopped working altogether, apparently reasoning that if the day was upon them, there was no point in continuing with ordinary life.

Paul writes with unusual urgency to address both the false teaching and its practical consequences. His response to the doctrinal error is one of the most detailed accounts of events preceding the Second Coming in the New Testament — the rebellion, the man of lawlessness, the restrainer, the strong delusion. His response to the practical error is one of the most direct ethical instructions in all his letters: if anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat. The two problems are connected: a false eschatology produces disordered living; a true eschatology produces ordered, purposeful, patiently working discipleship.

Did Paul write this letter? Some scholars doubt it, because it is so like 1 Thessalonians in wording yet seems to speak differently about the end: there the day comes suddenly, here certain events must come first. But the letter was received as Paul’s from the earliest days, it closes with his own signature, This is the sign of genuineness in every letter of mine (3:17), and the two pictures fit together: the day will surprise the unprepared, yet God has set what must precede it. The more likely conclusion is that Paul wrote it, within months of the first letter, to correct a misunderstanding of it.

The letter is framed by two great convictions. The first is the righteous judgment of God (chapter 1): those who afflict the Thessalonians will face divine retribution; those who are afflicted will receive relief. The God who sees the suffering of his people does not leave it unanswered. The second is the faithfulness of God (chapter 3): 'The Lord is faithful. He will establish you and guard you against the evil one' (3:3). Between the sovereign judgment of the first chapter and the guarding faithfulness of the last runs the most extraordinary theological disclosure of the letter — the mystery of lawlessness, the restrainer, and the man of lawlessness whose coming precedes the Lord's. Paul does not explain everything; he explains enough to steady the congregation and call them back to the settled, working, praying life of those who know their God and wait for his Son.

1.title: Relief Is Coming
1.overview:
Within months of his first letter, Paul writes again. The persecution in Thessalonica has grown worse, someone is claiming (perhaps in Paul’s name) that the day of the Lord has already come, and some believers have stopped working. Chapter 1 steadies a suffering church before any correction comes.

Then he answers the question suffering always raises: will wrong go unanswered? No. The answer comes on the day the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The same three men, the same church, the same grace and peace: a shaken congregation is first told that nothing at the foundation has moved.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why a Second Letter So Soon

Paul lays the foundation before the correction: grace and peace from God our Father, and everything hard in the letter sits inside that frame (3:16, 18).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A church squeezed by hostility outside and a rumour inside is first told where it is: in God our Father.

Now: A frightened congregation cannot hear correction until it has been steadied, and the steadying is doctrinal rather than emotional.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, To the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Chapter 1 meets a persecuted church with the coming of its King. Paul thanks God that their faith and love are growing under pressure (vv. 1–4). Their endurance is evidence of God’s just judgement: he will count them worthy of his kingdom and repay their persecutors (vv. 5–6). That will happen when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven in flaming fire, punishing those who do not know God or obey the gospel with eternal destruction away from his presence, and being glorified in his saints (vv. 7–10). So Paul prays that God will make them worthy of his calling, so that Christ’s name is glorified in them, and they in him (vv. 11–12).

The setting. Written a few months after 1 Thessalonians, probably also from Corinth around AD 51 (Acts 18:11). Word had reached Paul that the Thessalonians were being told the day of the Lord had already come (2:2), and worse, that the claim was circulating under his own name, perhaps in a forged letter. The persecution had intensified. And the idleness he had warned about in the first letter had hardened into a real problem (3:6–12).

Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy. The greeting is almost word for word what he wrote before, and the repetition is the point. The same three men: Paul; Silvanus, the Silas of Acts, who had been beaten and jailed with Paul at Philippi just before they reached Thessalonica (Acts 16:19–24; 17:1–4); and Timothy, whom Paul had sent back to strengthen them (1 Thessalonians 3:2). The same church. The same grace and peace. A congregation thrown into confusion is being told, before any argument begins, that nothing at the foundation has moved.

In God our Father. One small change from the first letter is worth catching. There he wrote in God the Father (1 Thessalonians 1:1); here it is in God our Father, a single word that gathers founders and harassed congregation alike under one fatherhood. And the address makes a claim about location: not in Thessalonica, where the pressure was, nor in the confusion, where their minds were, but in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Paul tells them where they actually are before he tells them anything else, and he sets the Father and the Son side by side as the one sphere in which a church lives. A Jew raised to say the LORD is one would not place a mere man beside God like that. What does it mean to be in God and in Christ? It means being the Father’s children and joined to the Son, so that nothing in Thessalonica or anywhere else can separate you from that love (Romans 8:38–39). You are not chiefly in your workplace, your diagnosis or your argument.

Grace and peace from the Father and the Son. Grace is God’s undeserved favour, the whole of his kindness given to people who had earned the opposite. Peace is what that favour produces: reconciliation with God, made by the blood of his Son’s cross (Colossians 1:20), and the settled wholeness that flows from it. Both come equally from the Father and the Son, one source named twice. And both nouns are about to be tested. This letter contains flaming fire, a man of lawlessness, a strong delusion, and a congregation told to withdraw from some of its own members. It opens with grace and peace, and it will close the same way (3:16, 18). Everything hard sits inside that frame. The church was not at peace outwardly, but Paul’s greeting is not a pleasantry; it is a delivery of the thing their circumstances could not take away.

Why does Paul repeat almost exactly what he wrote before? Because frightened people need to hear that the ground has not shifted. Someone had told the Thessalonians that the end had come and they had missed it, and had used Paul’s name to say so (2:2). The quickest way to steady them was to sound exactly like himself: the same men, the same names for God, the same blessing. Repetition in Scripture is rarely filler. When God says the same thing twice, it is because his people need it twice, and Christians who have heard the gospel a thousand times still need the thousand-and-first.

For worship. Our Father does not change his greeting when his children are in trouble. He speaks the same grace and the same peace over the frightened church that he spoke over the flourishing one, because neither was ever based on how they were doing. The Father who gave his Son, and the Son who gave himself, stand together at the head of this letter as the one fountain of every blessing, and nothing in the fire or the confusion that follows will reach back far enough to dry it up.
verseByVerse.note: Written soon after 1 Thessalonians, probably also from Corinth, to a church still under persecution and now confused about the day of the Lord.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Thanksgiving for a church standing under persecution (vv. 3–4) leads to the day when that persecution is answered: rest for the afflicted and ruin for those who refuse God, when the Lord Jesus is revealed (vv. 5–10). Paul then prays toward that day (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgment as Justice

Repayment rests on God's justice, not his temper (v. 6). Because God has undertaken to judge, Christians may never take revenge (Romans 12:19). Verse 9's ‘eternal destruction’ is read by some as final cessation; this commentary, with the historic Christian teaching, reads it as unending ruin, whose heart is exclusion ‘from the presence of the Lord’.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The promise of judgment was given to persecuted people not as a licence for revenge but as its removal: let God judge, and endure.

Now: This doctrine is written for patience, not satisfaction, by a man with unceasing anguish for those outside (Romans 9:2–3).

verseByVerse.quote: We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, as is right, because your faith is growing abundantly, and the love of every one of you for one another is increasing. Therefore we ourselves boast about you in the churches of God for your steadfastness and faith in all your persecutions and in the afflictions that you are enduring.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We ought always. That is a curious way to open a thanksgiving, and it is different from the first letter, where he simply gave thanks. Here he says he is under obligation to. The word is opheilomen: we owe it, as one owes a debt. Thanking God for them is not flattery he might decline; it is a debt he has to pay, because of what God has visibly done. And the thanks goes not to the Thessalonians, but to God for them. Their growth is his work.

Growing abundantly. What God has done is stated in two verbs that both strain upward. The first is hyperauxanei, a compound found nowhere else in the New Testament: growing beyond, over-growing, the way a vine outruns its trellis. Paul had prayed for exactly this, that he might supply what was lacking in their faith (1 Thessalonians 3:10). God answered.

The love of every one. The second verb is pleonazei: overflowing, running past the brim. Paul had prayed for this too, that the Lord would make them increase and abound in love for one another (1 Thessalonians 3:12). The detail in the middle matters: the love of every one of you. Not the love of the congregation in general, which anyone can say about a church, but of each person, in a community under enough external pressure to make people brittle. Persecuted groups often turn on each other. Fear makes people suspicious, and suffering makes them short. This one was not turning in; it was overflowing outward.

We ourselves boast. The pronoun is emphatic. Paul, who insisted to these very people that he never sought glory from anyone (1 Thessalonians 2:6), goes round the churches telling other congregations what God is doing in Thessalonica.

Steadfastness and faith. See what he boasts of, because it is not their numbers or their gifts or their buildings. It is their steadfastness, hypomonē, the endurance that stays under a load without putting it down, and their faith, which here leans toward faithfulness: still trusting, still loyal. The participle is present: the afflictions are still going on as he writes. He is not circulating a success story about a church that came through. He is telling other congregations about people who are, at that moment, still under it and still standing. That is a quiet rebuke to the way we measure churches, and ourselves: we reach for size and visible success, and God looks for faithfulness under strain. The persecution itself is not good; it is the sin of those who inflict it, and v. 6 says God will repay it. But God uses it the way a gardener uses the very wind that bends a young tree to drive its roots deeper.

The steadfastness of Christ. Where does a frightened young church get endurance like this? Paul names the source later in the letter, praying that the Lord would direct their hearts to the love of God and to the steadfastness of Christ (3:5), the same word. Their endurance is borrowed. Christ stayed under the load laid on him all the way to the cross without putting it down, and for the joy set before him endured it (Hebrews 12:2). Joined to him, his people endure with his endurance. What Paul boasts of in the churches is, at bottom, the Lord Jesus made visible in a persecuted congregation: his patience and his faithfulness showing through people who could never have produced them.

Is it right to boast about a church? Doesn’t that feed pride? It depends on what is being boasted about and to whom the credit goes. Paul has just thanked God for this growth; his boasting is the public side of his thanksgiving, telling others what God has done (compare 1 Corinthians 1:31). He does not praise their talent but their endurance, which is the Spirit’s fruit. Boasting of that kind encourages weaker churches, honours God, and lets struggling believers know their faithfulness has been seen. What would be wrong is boasting in size, prestige or our own cleverness, or praising people in a way that hides the God behind them.

My faith doesn’t feel as if it is growing. What then? Growth is rarely visible from inside, and often seen first by others. The Thessalonians probably felt anything but strong; they were frightened and confused, and Paul still saw their faith over-growing. Measure growth not by feelings of strength but by what is still standing: you are still praying, still coming back to Christ, still loving people who are hard to love, still holding on under pressure you did not choose. That holding is growth. And ask God for it, as Paul did for them, because it is his gift before it is your achievement.

On a Tuesday. Think of one believer you know who is under pressure and still standing: an illness, a hostile workplace, a hard marriage, a family that mocks their faith. Thank God for them by name today, and then tell them what you see. Paul did not keep his admiration for the Thessalonians private; he let them know that others knew. A single sentence from you may be the evidence someone needs that their endurance is not invisible.

verseByVerse.quote: This is evidence of the righteous judgment of God, that you may be considered worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you are also suffering—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Evidence of the righteous judgment. This is easy to misread. What is evidence? Not the persecution itself: God is not vindicated by the fact that his people are being hurt. The nearest antecedent is what he has just described, their steadfastness and faith under it. Their endurance is the exhibit. The word endeigma means a proof or plain indication, the kind of evidence that settles a case. Ordinary people holding their ground under sustained hostility need explaining, and the explanation is that God is at work in them and will vindicate them. It is the same logic he used with the Philippians, whose fearlessness he called a clear sign of their salvation, and that from God (Philippians 1:28). Nobody stands like that over nothing.

Considered worthy. The word (kataxiōthēnai) means counted worthy, judged fit. Worthiness here is not merit earned by suffering, as if the more a believer suffered the surer his place; that would contradict everything Paul teaches, and he will pray later in the chapter that God would make them worthy (v. 11), which he would not need to do if they were achieving it themselves. It is fittedness. God does not decide their suffering has earned them a place; he declares them fit for the kingdom he is pleased to give (Luke 12:32), and their endurance proves the faith he gave them is real.

For which you are also suffering. They suffer because they belong to God’s kingdom. Paul had told new converts in Galatia that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (Acts 14:22), and he had warned the Thessalonians in person that they were destined for affliction (1 Thessalonians 3:3–4). Their affliction is not random misfortune that God is making the best of. They are suffering for the thing they are being fitted for. That is a stronger sentence than God will bring good out of this.

Suffering, then glory. The road these believers are on was walked first by their King. Was it not necessary, the risen Jesus asked, that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? (Luke 24:26). Suffering then glory is the shape of his own story, and Paul says elsewhere that we are heirs with Christ, provided we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him (Romans 8:17). So their affliction is not a detour from the kingdom. It is the King’s own road, and walking it marks them as his. The apostles left the council rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name (Acts 5:41): the same thought, from the same Lord. The world reads such pain as evidence that their God is weak or absent. Paul reads it the other way round: a God who was absent would have left them to collapse, and they have not collapsed.

In the flow. Verse 5 is where the chapter turns. Verses 3–4 thanked God for a church standing under pressure; verses 6–10 will draw back the curtain on the day when that pressure is answered. And this prepares the correction of chapter 2: if God’s righteous judgement is still ahead, at the revealing of Christ, then the day of the Lord cannot already have come while they are still suffering.

What about suffering that has nothing to do with my faith, like illness or grief? This verse speaks specifically of suffering for the kingdom: hostility because you belong to Christ. But the wider truth reaches further. Scripture teaches that God works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28), and that every trial a believer endures is used by the Father to refine and train (Hebrews 12:5–11; 1 Peter 1:6–7). Your illness is not persecution, and you need not call it that. But the endurance God gives you in it is still his work, still evidence of grace, and still preparing you for the kingdom where there will be no more pain.

On a Tuesday. The colleague who freezes you out because you will not join the joke, the relative who sneers at your faith, the promotion that went elsewhere because you would not shade the truth: none of it is a sign that God has forgotten you. It is the old mark of citizenship. Do not go looking for suffering, and do not dramatise ordinary friction. But when it comes because of Christ, do not be ashamed. Thank him that you are counted among those who bear his name.

verseByVerse.quote: since indeed God considers it just to repay with affliction those who afflict you, and to grant relief to you who are afflicted as well as to us, when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his mighty angels
verseByVerse.commentary:
God considers it just. Paul grounds what follows not in God’s anger but in his justice. The word is the righteousness word: this is what a fair verdict looks like. That distinction matters, because divine judgement is often imagined as a loss of temper. It is the opposite. A judge who let cruelty pass without response would not be merciful; he would be unjust, and we would say so about any human court. The people afflicting the Thessalonians had made choices, and those choices had victims. There will be an accounting, and it is the work of a good God rather than a provoked one.

Relief. The symmetry is exact and deliberate: affliction repaid to the afflicters, and to the afflicted, relief. The word is anesis: a loosening, a slackening of tension, rest, release. It is what happens when a strained rope is let out, or a besieged city is relieved. And note the words he adds: as well as to us. Paul puts himself on the same side of the ledger. He is not an official announcing an outcome from a safe distance; he is another man waiting for the same rest.

Revealed from heaven. The timing is everything: relief comes when the Lord Jesus is revealed. Not before. Paul does not promise the persecution will stop, and as far as we know it did not. What he gives them is a date they cannot see and cannot hurry, which is a harder comfort than deliverance next month and a far more durable one. “Revealed” is apokalypsis: an unveiling, the drawing back of a curtain on something that was there all along. Nothing is being created on that day; something is being shown. The Lord these people already serve, and the justice they cannot presently see, will simply become visible.

With his mighty angels. Literally, the angels of his power. They accompany him as his army and his servants (Matthew 13:41; 25:31). The one who was arrested in a garden, and who said he could have called on more than twelve legions of angels and did not (Matthew 26:53), returns with them at his command.

One coming, not two. Look at what happens at this one unveiling: relief for the afflicted church and judgement on its afflicters, together, on the same day, in public, from heaven. Paul knows of no earlier, secret coming in which believers are quietly removed before the trouble. Their rest begins at the same visible revelation at which the persecutors are repaid. That is why this commentary reads the Lord’s return as a single, glorious, public event at the end of the age, bringing the resurrection, the gathering of the saints and the final judgement together (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; Matthew 25:31–32). Many faithful Christians, especially in churches shaped by dispensational teaching (which expects a secret rapture of the church before a final period of tribulation), read the prophecies differently, and they love the Lord’s appearing as truly as anyone. The hope of the church is not escape from the world’s last troubles but the appearing of its King.

Is it wrong to want God to punish those who have hurt me? Wanting justice is not wrong: the souls under the altar cry out for it (Revelation 6:10), and the psalms are full of the cry. What is wrong is wanting to take it yourself, or wanting the person to be lost rather than repent. A Christian holds both: a real longing for wrong to be put right, handed over to God, and a real prayer that the one who did it might be converted, as Saul the persecutor was. Paul himself was once on the other side of this verse. Leave the verdict to the Judge, and pray for the defendant. The believer who knows God is just is the only person who can afford to be gentle (Romans 12:19–21).

Why does God let persecution go on so long? Because his patience is giving time for repentance, including the repentance of persecutors (2 Peter 3:9), and because he is doing something in his suffering people that comfort could not do (v. 5). The delay is not neglect. The Thessalonians did not see the end in their lifetimes, and their persecutors may have died unrepaid by any human court. But the date is fixed, and no case is closed until the Judge closes it.

verseByVerse.quote: in flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and on those who do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In flaming fire. Fire is the standing Old Testament image for God made visible and for his holy judgement: the bush that burned and was not consumed (Exodus 3:2), the pillar that went before Israel, the mountain at Sinai wrapped in smoke because the LORD had descended on it in fire (Exodus 19:18), the LORD who will come in fire to render his anger (Isaiah 66:15), and the Ancient of Days whose throne was fiery flames (Daniel 7:9–10). Paul is not inventing a new picture; he is putting Jesus where the God of Sinai stood.

Inflicting vengeance. “Vengeance” is a word modern readers wince at, and the wince deserves a hearing. It translates ekdikēsis: just punishment, justice carried out by the one authorised to carry it out. It is not personal spite. Paul forbids personal revenge flatly (Romans 12:19), quoting the Lord’s word that vengeance is his, and that is exactly the point: it belongs to God, not to us, and here Christ himself carries it out. The whole reason a Christian can be told never to take revenge is that God has undertaken to see the matter dealt with.

Who do not know God. Paul names who this falls on, in two phrases, and the pairing is deliberate. The first is Old Testament language for the pagan world, the nations that do not know God (Psalm 79:6; Jeremiah 10:25). These are not people who never had any light. Paul taught that what can be known about God is plain to everyone, and that people suppress it (Romans 1:18–21, 28). Not knowing God, in Scripture, is not innocent ignorance but a refusal of the knowledge that was available, and each is judged by the light he was given (Romans 2:12).

Who do not obey the gospel. The second phrase describes people who have heard the message and refused it. Between them the two phrases cover everyone, the uninformed and the informed, under one verdict. And do not miss the verb: not those who do not believe the gospel but those who do not obey it. Paul uses it more than once (Romans 10:16). The gospel is not merely an offer to be considered on its merits. It is the announcement that God has installed his Son as King, and it comes with a command: God commands all people everywhere to repent (Acts 17:30). To shrug at it is not neutrality; it is a refusal.

What about people who have never heard the gospel? They are not judged for rejecting a gospel they never heard; they are judged for refusing the God they did know, in creation and conscience (Romans 1:20; 2:14–16). But the Bible gives no hope that anyone is saved apart from Christ: there is salvation in no one else (Acts 4:12), and people call on him only when they hear (Romans 10:13–15). That is why this verse should send the church to the nations, not into speculation. We leave the hidden judgements to a God who is perfectly just, and we do what he commanded: go and tell.

What does it mean to obey the gospel? It means to do what the gospel calls for: to repent of sin and trust Jesus Christ as Saviour and Lord. Obedience here is not earning salvation by good works; it is the obedience of faith (Romans 1:5), bowing to the King by receiving him. From that first obedience flows a life of following him, imperfectly and truly. The person who believes the gospel obeys it; the person who refuses to come has disobeyed it, however politely.

On a Tuesday. The gospel is not a brochure to be filed but a King’s summons. If you have been keeping him at arm’s length, considering him, admiring him, postponing him, recognise that as disobedience to a King, and come. And if you have come, think of one person who does not know God, pray for them by name, and ask whether they have ever heard the gospel from you clearly enough to obey it.

For worship. The fire of Sinai now burns around the Lord Jesus, and it is his right. He is the God who came down on the mountain, and the God who came down in the manger, and he will come again in flaming fire as the rightful King of all the earth. Yet the same Lord who will command the fire once stood under it in our place, so that everyone who obeys the gospel finds that the fire has already fallen on him, and has nothing left to burn.

parallels.desc: the LORD will come in fire

verseByVerse.quote: They will suffer the punishment of eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his might,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eternal destruction. “Punishment” (dikē) means penalty, justice: what is due. This is among the most solemn sentences Paul wrote, and it should be handled without relish. “Eternal” (aiōnios) is the word used for eternal life: the age-to-come word, everlasting. Jesus sets eternal punishment and eternal life side by side in one sentence (Matthew 25:46). “Destruction” (olethros) means ruin, undoing, the loss of everything good. It does not by itself mean annihilation. Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians 5:5 of a man handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, and that man goes on existing and is expected to be restored. The ruin is a state, and the word eternal tells us it is never reversed.

Away from the presence. This is the clause to weigh. “Presence” is literally face, and the phrase echoes Isaiah 2, where men hide from before the terror of the LORD and from the splendour of his majesty. The Greek preposition behind away from (apo) can carry two senses here: a destruction that comes from his face, and a destruction that shuts people away from it. Both are true, and read as the ESV reads it, the clause defines the punishment as an exclusion: shut out from the face of God, the source of all joy, light and life. Hell is not most deeply a chamber of torments but an absence. Every kindness, every beauty, every ordinary pleasure of a human life came from him, including for those who never acknowledged where it came from. To be finally away from him is to be away from all of it. Separated from his favour, though not from his justice: God is present in hell in his holiness, and absent in every blessing.

Depart from me. The Lord of this verse is the Lord Jesus of verse 7, and the words of exclusion are his own: depart from me (Matthew 7:23; 25:41). The one who will close the door is the one who wept over the city that would not come to him (Luke 19:41–42), and who said, Come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden (Matthew 11:28). Hell is, at its heart, to be finally without Christ, as heaven is, at its heart, to be always with the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17). No one will be shut out by a stranger. They will be shut out by the Saviour they refused. And the Son who will say those words is the Son who, on the cross, was himself forsaken, so that no one who trusts him ever will be.

Where Christians differ: eternal punishment or annihilation? Some (annihilationists or conditionalists, who hold that the lost are finally destroyed and cease to be; among them Edward Fudge, Clark Pinnock and, tentatively, John Stott) argue that eternal destruction means the wicked cease to exist, a destruction whose results are eternal. Universalists say all will eventually be saved. Those who hold these views include believers who love Scripture and argue from it, and the question is what the texts say. Verdict: Eternal destruction is everlasting, conscious ruin: exclusion from God’s gracious presence forever. The same word “eternal” describes both the punishment of the wicked and the life of the righteous (Matthew 25:46). Scripture speaks of the smoke of their torment rising forever and ever (Revelation 14:11; 20:10), and of unquenchable fire (Mark 9:43–48). This is the historic Christian teaching (the Westminster Confession 33.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 32.2). It is terrible, and should move believers to tears and to urgent evangelism, as it moved Paul (Romans 9:2–3).

How a Christian holds this. Two things should be said. First, Paul is not writing to gratify anyone’s appetite for the fate of their enemies. He is writing to people being hurt, to tell them that the wrong will not stand forever, and the effect he intends is patience, not satisfaction. God himself has no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live (Ezekiel 33:11). Second, this is written by a man who elsewhere says he has great sorrow and unceasing anguish in his heart for those outside, and could wish himself accursed for their sake (Romans 9:2–3). Anyone who can state this doctrine without grief has not understood it.

How can a God of love do this? Because love that is not also just is not love but indifference. A God who shrugged at cruelty, at the murder of children, at the oppression of the poor, at the contempt of his own Son, would not be kinder than the God of the Bible; he would be morally smaller. Hell is God giving people, finally and justly, what they chose: life without him. And the measure of his love is not that there is no judgement, but that he sent his Son to bear it for all who would come (Romans 5:8). Scripture never pictures anyone who wanted God being turned away from him (John 6:37).

Is endless punishment fair for sins committed in a short life? The weight of a wrong is measured not by how long it took but by whom it was against: striking a stranger and striking a king are not the same act. Sin is committed against the infinitely holy God, who is owed all our love, and so it is far heavier than it feels to us. Nor is the punishment the same for all: the one who knew his master’s will and ignored it is judged more severely than the one who did not know (Luke 12:47–48). We may not see every reason yet, but we can rest on this: the Judge of all the earth will do what is just (Genesis 18:25).

How can I be happy in heaven if someone I love is lost? This is one of the hardest questions a Christian asks, and Scripture does not give every detail. What it promises is that God will wipe away every tear (Revelation 21:4), and that on that day we will see his justice as clearly as his mercy, and will not find him wrong in anything. We will love what he loves, and agree with him completely. For now, the question should not paralyse you but propel you: while they live, the door is open. Pray for them, speak to them, and leave in God’s hands what only he can judge.

On a Tuesday. Let this verse do what Paul meant it to do: give you patience when you are wronged, and courage to speak, kindly and soon, to someone who is drifting from God. And if you read it and fear it describes you, that fear is not the mark of the people in this verse, who do not know God and do not care to; it is a summons to the Saviour who has promised never to cast out anyone who comes.

verseByVerse.quote: when he comes on that day to be glorified in his saints, and to be marveled at among all who have believed, because our testimony to you was believed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To be glorified in his saints. The preposition is the whole point. He is glorified in them, not merely by them. His glory will be seen in the people he rescued, in what he has made of them: they are the mirror, not the light. Think about who Paul is saying this to. A small, harassed congregation in a provincial city, meeting in somebody’s house, despised by their neighbours, with some of their number already buried (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Paul tells them that when the Lord Jesus is revealed in flaming fire with his mighty angels, what everyone will be looking at is them, and in them, him. The same day that brings ruin to some is the day of his glory in his people.

Marveled at. A strong verb: to be wondered at, to cause astonishment. Believers will marvel at him, overwhelmed with wonder. Paul names them as the ones marvelling, though the angels, who long to look into these things (1 Peter 1:12), may well share it. The language echoes the psalms, where God is greatly feared in the council of the holy ones (Psalm 89:7) and awesome from his sanctuary (Psalm 68:35). And the wonder is not at the saints’ achievement. It is at what grace did with such material. If you have ever thought your own case too far gone or too ordinary to be worth much, this verse says the finished work will be a thing that stops heaven in its tracks.

Our testimony was believed. The final clause is easy to skip, and it is the link that connects the cosmic scene to a particular week in Thessalonica. Why will these people be among those in whom Christ is glorified? Because probably not much more than a year earlier three travelling men said something in their town and they believed it. The whole blazing revelation, angels, fire, glory, the settling of every account, reaches these people through a testimony that was spoken and received. Paul will ask them in the next chapter to hold to what they were taught (2:15), and this is why. The last day runs through the ordinary act of believing what was said to you.

Who are the saints? All who have believed. Paul puts the two phrases side by side: his saints, and all who have believed. Saint means holy one, someone set apart for God, and in the New Testament it is the ordinary name for every Christian (1 Corinthians 1:2). It is not a rank achieved by a few extraordinary people or conferred after death. If you trust Christ, you are one of the saints in whom he will be glorified, not because you are impressive but because he is.

On a Tuesday. Look at the most unremarkable believer in your church, perhaps the one you find hardest to love, and then look in the mirror. Both of you are going to be part of the display of Christ’s glory on the last day. Treat one another accordingly. And when you are tempted to think your faith is too small to matter, remember the link: you believed the testimony. That is all the Thessalonians did, and it put them in the centre of the last day.

For worship. He will not be glorified in spite of his people, nor beside them, but in them: the rescued, the remade, the once-dead now shining with a light that is entirely his. And the wonder has already begun: the astonishment of that day is only the eyes of faith opened wide.

verseByVerse.quote: To this end we always pray for you, that our God may make you worthy of his calling and may fulfill every resolve for good and every work of faith by his power, so that the name of our Lord Jesus may be glorified in you, and you in him, according to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We always pray. Having described the day, Paul prays toward it. The coming of Christ is not, for Paul, a subject for charts; it is a reason to pray.

Make you worthy. This petition settles the question v. 5 raised: the worthiness is something asked of God, not earned. The endurance he praised in v. 4 he now requests from God in v. 11. God called them; may he make them live up to it (Ephesians 4:1). The calling is God’s effectual summons, the call that does not merely invite but actually brings a person, by which he drew them to Christ through the gospel (2:14), and the God who called is the God who completes.

Every resolve for good. Two things he asks God to bring to completion. The first is the inward decision, the good intention formed, every desire for goodness God has planted in them. It is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:13).

Every work of faith. The second is the thing actually done, every action springing from faith (1 Thessalonians 1:3). Paul knows how often the first dies before it reaches the second, the resolve made on Sunday and gone by Wednesday, and he asks God to carry both through. And he says how it happens: by his power, the power of the Spirit God gives to his people (1 Thessalonians 4:8), not by their determination.

Glorified in you, and you in him. Verse 12 gives the purpose, and it is a two-way sentence. His name means his person and reputation, all that he is. The first half we might have expected: the aim of Christian living is his honour, seen in his people, which is exactly v. 10. The second half is astonishing and Paul does not pause over it. The traffic runs both ways. Whatever glory they receive is not a separate award handed out alongside his; it is his own, shared with the people joined to him. On that day believers will be raised with bodies like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21), and they will be like him, because they will see him as he is (1 John 3:2). They do not become divine. They shine with a borrowed light, as the moon shines with the sun’s.

According to the grace. The last clause keeps the whole thing where the letter began. Not according to their endurance, which has been considerable and which Paul has boasted about in the churches, but according to grace, from beginning to end. The measure of what they receive is set by the giver’s generosity, not by the quality of their standing under pressure. Some read the phrase as our God and Lord, Jesus Christ, calling Jesus God directly; the Greek can be taken either way. Either way, grace comes from both, and a Jewish monotheist would not name a man as the joint source of God’s grace unless the Son shared the Father’s deity.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul doubts they will make it, or that their calling hangs on their effort. He prays because God keeps his called people through means, and prayer is one of them.

If God does it all by his power, what do I do? You do the resolving and the working; God gives the power to do them. Paul prays for their resolve for good and their work of faith; both are really theirs. Grace does not make us passive; it makes us able. So you form good intentions and act on them, and you pray as you do, because the gap between Sunday’s resolution and Wednesday’s action is exactly where you need him. When a good desire stirs in you, to forgive, to give, to speak to a neighbour about Christ, treat it as something God may be starting, ask him to finish it, and take the first step today.

On a Tuesday. This is a prayer to borrow. Most of us carry a small pile of good intentions that never reached Wednesday: the letter not written, the visit not made, the apology still rehearsed. Paul does not scold the pile. He prays over it, to a God whose power is the difference between a resolve and a deed. Christ’s own obedience never stalled between the two, and it is counted as yours (Romans 5:19); so you may pray over your pile without dread, and over someone you love.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, To the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ:<sup>2</sup>Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.<sup>3</sup>We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, as is right, because your faith is growing abundantly, and the love of every one of you for one another is increasing.<sup>4</sup>Therefore we ourselves boast about you in the churches of God for your steadfastness and faith in all your persecutions and in the afflictions that you are enduring.<sup>5</sup>This is evidence of the righteous judgment of God, that you may be considered worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you are also suffering—<sup>6</sup>since indeed God considers it just to repay with affliction those who afflict you,<sup>7</sup>and to grant relief to you who are afflicted as well as to us, when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his mighty angels<sup>8</sup>in flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and on those who do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus.<sup>9</sup>They will suffer the punishment of eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his might,<sup>10</sup>when he comes on that day to be glorified in his saints, and to be marveled at among all who have believed, because our testimony to you was believed.<sup>11</sup>To this end we always pray for you, that our God may make you worthy of his calling and may fulfill every resolve for good and every work of faith by his power,<sup>12</sup>so that the name of our Lord Jesus may be glorified in you, and you in him, according to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus Christ.

2.title: The Mystery of Lawlessness
2.overview:
Someone had told the Thessalonians, perhaps by a forged letter in Paul’s name, that the day of the Lord had already come. To a persecuted church promised relief on that day (1:7), this was devastating: either the promise had failed, or they had been passed over. Paul answers with an argument they can check: the day cannot have come, because two things must happen first, the great rebellion and the revealing of the “man of lawlessness”, who sets himself up in God’s place. Something now restrains him; when it is removed he will appear, deceive those who refused to love the truth, and be destroyed by the Lord Jesus with a breath.

Paul had taught this in person (v. 5), so he writes in shorthand, and some details (above all the restrainer) are now uncertain. The pastoral point is plain: the worst coming evil runs on God’s timetable and ends at Christ’s coming. Then Paul turns to thanks and to a call to stand firm.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul answers the claim that the day has come with what must happen first: the rebellion, the man of lawlessness, the restraint that holds him back for now, and his swift end at the Lord’s coming (vv. 1–12).
verseByVerse.theology:
Judicial Hardening

God sends the delusion of verse 11 ‘therefore’ because they refused to love the truth (v. 10). It is a judicial response to a prior refusal, and it locates the failure in the affections, not the intellect: which is also why signs and wonders prove nothing on their own.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul’s cure for a panicked church was not a newer prediction but an argument they could check for themselves.

Now: Paul gives a pattern to recognise, not a name to guess, and the build-up ends with the Lord undoing the lawless one with a breath (v. 8).

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our being gathered together to him, we ask you, brothers, not to be quickly shaken in mind or alarmed, either by a spirit or a spoken word, or a letter seeming to be from us, to the effect that the day of the Lord has come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 2 Thessalonians 2 corrects a false teaching that the day of the Lord had already come. Paul says: do not be shaken. That day will not come until the rebellion, a great falling away, and the revealing of the man of lawlessness, who will claim to be God. Something now restrains him, though the mystery of lawlessness is already at work. When he is revealed, with Satanic power and false wonders that deceive those who refused to love the truth, the Lord Jesus will destroy him by the breath of his mouth and the splendour of his coming (vv. 1–12). By contrast, the Thessalonians were chosen for salvation and called through the gospel to share Christ’s glory; so they are to stand firm and hold to the apostolic teaching (vv. 13–17). The darkest chapter in the letter is written to make frightened people calm: even the last rebellion runs on God’s timetable and ends with a single breath from Christ.

The coming of our Lord. Here is the emergency that produced the letter, and both phrases in the verse point straight back to the first letter. “Coming” is parousia: arrival, presence, the word used in the ancient world for the state visit of a king to a city. It is the coming of 1 Thessalonians 4:15. Paul is picking up exactly where he left off, because that is the teaching that had been twisted.

Our being gathered together. The word (episynagōgē) is precisely the scene of 1 Thessalonians 4:17: the dead raised and the living caught up to meet him in the air. It is the gathering of the elect from the four winds that Jesus promised at his coming (Matthew 24:31). Paul ties the two phrases together under one article, presenting the coming and the gathering as one event, not two. And the gathering is to him: the hope is not a place or an escape but a Person, at whose side his people will always be.

Shaken in mind or alarmed. The first verb is saleuthēnai, to be shaken, the word Luke uses of an earthquake rocking a prison’s foundations (Acts 16:26). The second, throeisthai, is a continuous present: not a single fright but an ongoing state of panic. That is what false teaching about the end does to a church: knocks it off its foundations, then keeps it rattled. And the word quickly matters. Paul is not surprised that a lie was told; he is grieved at how fast they let it move them.

A spirit, a word, or a letter. A spirit: a claimed prophecy, an utterance in the meeting. A spoken word: a sermon, teaching, or report. A letter: perhaps forged in Paul’s name. He does not know which it was. The third is sobering. Someone had, or might have, written a letter pretending to be Paul in order to unsettle this congregation. That is why he signs this one in his own hand at the end and calls it the sign of genuineness in every letter of his (3:17). Within twenty-odd years of the resurrection, Paul already thought it possible that his mail was being counterfeited.

The day of the Lord has come. What the message claimed is the crux. The verb is enestēken, a perfect: it has arrived and is now present. Not that it is near, which is what Paul himself taught, but that it is here already and they had somehow missed it. Perhaps the teachers said it had begun spiritually, or that the persecution was the proof. That was devastating rather than merely mistaken. These people had been promised relief when the Lord was revealed (1:7). If the day had already come and this was it, still hunted, still burying friends, no vindication, then either the promise had failed or they had been passed over. No wonder they were shaken. Paul does not cure the panic by telling them to stop thinking about the Lord’s return; he cures it by teaching them about it properly.

Does this rule out a secret rapture before the tribulation? Pretribulational Christians hold that the church will be taken away before the day of the Lord begins, and that the man of lawlessness will appear only after it has gone. But Paul treats the coming, the gathering and the day as one event, and he tells the Thessalonians that day will not come until the rebellion and the man of lawlessness appear (v. 3), which reads most naturally if they will still be here to see them. If a secret removal were the next thing on the calendar, this was the moment to say so, and it would have been the simplest comfort in the world. He says nothing of the kind. The more likely reading is that there is one public return of Christ, at which he gathers his people and judges the lawless one (v. 8). Christians who hold the other view are our brothers, and we can hold this charitably; but the church should not expect to be spared the last troubles. It should expect to be kept through them.

How should I respond to end-times predictions today? With calm and with your Bible. Paul’s remedy for the Thessalonians was not a newer, better prediction but a return to what they had been taught. When someone announces that recent events prove the end is upon us, or names a date, or claims a special revelation about the timetable, ask the questions Paul would ask: does Scripture say this, or only the speaker? Does it make me more faithful, or only more anxious? Jesus said no one knows the day or hour (Matthew 24:36), and every date ever set has been wrong. Be ready every day, and unsettled by no one.

On a Tuesday. Think about what you have been reading or watching about the future, and what it has done to you. If it has left you agitated, fascinated or fearful rather than steady, prayerful and kind, it has not been doing what Paul’s teaching does. Turn it off, and read 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18 and this chapter instead.

For worship. The coming of our Lord Jesus Christ is not a rumour that can be counterfeited or a date that can slip by unnoticed. When the King comes, no one will need to be told; and when he gathers his people, not one of them will be missing. The day has not passed us by. He is still coming, and he will come for us.
verseByVerse.note: Someone was claiming — perhaps even by a forged letter — that the day of the Lord had already come.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one deceive you in any way. For that day will not come, unless the rebellion comes first, and the man of lawlessness is revealed, the son of destruction,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let no one deceive you. Blunt: whatever the channel, whatever the credentials. When Jesus taught about the last things, his very first word was a warning against deception, and he came back to it again and again: see that no one leads you astray, for many will come in my name (Matthew 24:4–5, 11, 24).

The rebellion comes first. Now Paul’s argument, and its shape matters. He gives them a checkable fact: certain things must happen first, and they plainly have not. Therefore the day has not come. It is an argument any of them could run without him, which is exactly what a frightened church needs. The first event is hē apostasia, with the article, the apostasy, a specific and expected event. The word means defection, falling away, revolt, and the Greek Old Testament uses it of turning away from God. Paul assumes they know what he means, because he had told them (v. 5).

Which reading of the rebellion is most likely? The rebellion is most likely a great falling away from the faith within the professing church, as Jesus foretold, when the love of many will grow cold (Matthew 24:10–12), and as Paul warns elsewhere: in later times some will depart from the faith (1 Timothy 4:1). It may be joined to an open revolt of the world against God, but its heart is defection by those who once professed to belong. It is the climax of a defection already at work (v. 7).

The man of lawlessness. Note the verb: revealed, apokalyphthē, the same word used of Christ’s own appearing in 1:7. Paul uses it three times of this figure in this passage. It is a deliberate parody, a dark mirror of the real unveiling. “Lawlessness” (anomia) is the rejection of God’s law. The phrase names his essence: not merely someone who breaks laws, but one whose principle is the abolition of God’s law and of any authority above himself. He is very probably the figure John calls the antichrist (1 John 2:18). Many manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read man of sin, as the ESV notes; the meaning is the same.

The obedient Son. The lawless one is best understood against the one he counterfeits. Christ is the Son who came into the world saying, I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart (Psalm 40:8; Hebrews 10:5–7). He kept the law his people broke, and obeyed to the point of death, and his obedience is counted to all who trust him (Romans 5:19). Sin has always been lawlessness (1 John 3:4), and in this last figure the whole history of human rebellion comes to a head, as the whole of human obedience came to a head in Jesus. That is why the rebellion is a falling away: it is defection from him. The last days set the lawless man beside the obedient Son, and the end of each is already written.

The son of destruction. A Hebrew idiom: one destined for destruction, who belongs to ruin. The only other person in the New Testament called that is Judas (John 17:12), which is its own quiet commentary: the last great enemy and the betrayer share a name, and both of them, for all their apparent power, end where God said they would. On the night he was betrayed, Jesus could tell his Father that he had guarded those given to him, and not one was lost but the son of destruction; and he guards them still.

Where Christians differ: who is the man of lawlessness? Interpretations include: a Roman emperor of Paul’s own time; the papacy, as most of the Reformers held (the original Westminster Confession 25.6 named the Pope as antichrist, and the 1689 London Baptist Confession 26.4 does the same); a principle of evil throughout history rather than a person; or a single individual who will appear just before Christ’s return. Verdict: Paul describes a person (“man,” “he”), revealed at a particular time, destroyed at Christ’s coming (v. 8). So the best reading is that he is a final individual, the climactic embodiment of rebellion against God, appearing at the end of the age just before Christ’s return. Yet the mystery of lawlessness is already at work (v. 7), and many antichrists have come (1 John 2:18): throughout history, persons and powers have shown his spirit, including religious systems that claim God’s authority for themselves. The Reformers rightly saw that spirit at work in the abuses of their day. Believers should not speculate about names, but stay faithful and discerning.

A caution about names. Christians have identified this figure with a long series of candidates across twenty centuries, and every confident identification so far has been wrong. Nero, Muhammad, Napoleon, Hitler, Stalin: each was named by sincere believers as the man of sin, and each died without being destroyed by the appearing of Christ. That record should make us modest. Paul gives a pattern to recognise, not a name to guess.

Does the great falling away mean true Christians can lose their salvation? No. Those who fall away are those who professed faith without possessing it. John says of such people: they went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2:19). Jesus says his sheep will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of his hand (John 10:28). The apostasy is real and terrible, and it should make every professing believer examine himself (2 Corinthians 13:5); but the elect are kept by God’s power through faith (1 Peter 1:5). Paul will say in v. 13 that these believers were chosen to be saved. The rebellion sifts the church; it does not defeat the Shepherd. And if the warning troubles you, let it send you to Christ rather than into despair: those who fear falling away and run to him are not the ones walking away.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ’s return is delayed indefinitely. These events could unfold quickly, and the spirit behind them is already at work. Paul is not giving them a reason to relax, but a reason not to panic.

On a Tuesday. Ask yourself what would keep you from falling away if many around you did. Not your upbringing, or your church’s size, or your circle of friends; those are exactly what shift when a great defection comes. Only Christ’s hold on you, and your hold on him, fed by his word and prayer, will stand (John 10:28). If your faith is mostly borrowed, go to him for yourself now, while the pressure is light.

verseByVerse.quote: who opposes and exalts himself against every so-called god or object of worship, so that he takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who opposes and exalts himself. The portrait is drawn in two strokes: what he opposes, and what he claims. He sets himself against all religion, true and false. This is not a rival religion. It is the abolition of religion as such, clearing the field so that nothing is left standing to be worshipped except himself. Paul is drawing on Daniel, and his readers would have heard it: the king who shall exalt himself and magnify himself above every god, and shall speak astonishing things against the God of gods (Daniel 11:36). Daniel’s prophecy found its first fulfilment in Antiochus Epiphanes, who in 167 BC set up an altar to Zeus in the Jerusalem temple, the abomination of desolation. Behind both stands the boast of the king of Babylon: I will ascend to heaven, I will make myself like the Most High (Isaiah 14:13–14).

He takes his seat. “Temple” (naos) is the inner sanctuary, the holy place itself, not the outer courts. And the seat is the point. He does not merely enter; he sits, which is what one does on a throne or in a place of settled authority.

Only one has the right to that seat. Scripture knows of one who rightly sat down in the presence of God. After making purification for sins, the Son sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high (Hebrews 1:3). The priests of the old temple stood daily at their service and never sat; Christ, having offered a single sacrifice for sins for all time, sat down at the right hand of God (Hebrews 10:11–12). The lawless one claims a seat he never earned and a deity he does not have, and he cannot make himself God by sitting in it. Christ took his seat because his work was finished and the deity was his from eternity. He did not grasp at equality with God but emptied himself (Philippians 2:6–7), and every knee, including the knee of the man of lawlessness, will bow to him.

Proclaiming himself to be God. The original sin taken to its extreme. The serpent’s offer was you will be like God (Genesis 3:5). Here is a man who accepts the offer publicly and requires everyone else to agree. And the Thessalonians did not have to imagine it. The Roman emperor Caligula had ordered his own statue set up in the Jerusalem temple in AD 40, about a decade earlier, and the empire came close to a Jewish war over it before he was assassinated. It was a recent memory, and it showed what Daniel meant.

Where Christians differ: which temple? Some take the temple of God to be a rebuilt Jewish temple in Jerusalem, where the antichrist will sit. Others take it as the church, God’s temple in the New Testament (1 Corinthians 3:16; 2 Corinthians 6:16), where false claims to divine authority arise; or as a picture of usurping God’s place. Verdict: The New Testament never predicts a rebuilt temple with divine approval; Christ is the true temple (John 2:19–21). The language most likely draws on Daniel’s imagery to describe the man of lawlessness usurping God’s place and claiming divine honours, perhaps within what claims to be the church. The point is clear whatever the location: he claims to be God. Christians need not look for a rebuilt temple as a sign.

The same material, smaller. The passage is not only about a figure at the end. Every smaller version of that claim, every self that sets itself above every authority and expects the world to arrange itself around it, is made of the same material. The tyrant who demands worship, the culture that says nothing is above the self, the church leader who will not be questioned, and the ordinary heart that says, in its own small kingdom, my will be done: all of them are rehearsals. In daily life it rarely looks like a throne. It looks like a man who cannot bear his plans to be interrupted, or a heart that lets its feelings decide what is right; and each small seat taken in God’s place can be handed back to him in a sentence of prayer.

Should we expect a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem as a sign of the end? No. Many Christians who do expect one are reading these words with real care, and the question does not touch the gospel. But if a temple were rebuilt, it would be a matter of politics and history, not a fulfilment of God’s plan, because the New Testament teaches that the sacrifices are finished in Christ (Hebrews 10:11–14, 18) and that God’s temple now is his people, built on Christ the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:19–22). Watching Jerusalem for building work is not what Paul asks of us. Watch instead for the thing he describes: a power that sets itself in God’s place and demands what belongs to God alone, especially when it does so in the name of religion.

parallels.desc: exalt himself and magnify himself above every god

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not remember that when I was still with you I told you these things?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not remember that when I was still with you I told you these things? Paul is not introducing new material. He is reminding them of teaching they had already received in person, slightly exasperated that he has to. They should have remembered and not been shaken.

I have told you beforehand. Paul is doing what his Lord did. Speaking of false christs and false signs, Jesus said, See, I have told you beforehand (Matthew 24:25); and in the upper room, I have told you before it takes place, so that when it does take place you may believe (John 14:29). Forewarning is how Christ shepherds frightened people. He does not hide the hard things to keep his disciples comfortable. He names them in advance, so that when they come they confirm his word instead of shaking it, and even the darkness of the last days becomes evidence that he knew, and that he is Lord of it.

One side of a conversation. That explains why the paragraph is so allusive. He writes the rebellion and the man of lawlessness and what is restraining him with definite articles and no explanation, because his readers had heard him spell it out. We are reading one side of a conversation whose other half was spoken aloud in a Macedonian house and never written down. That is the honest reason the restrainer in the next verses is obscure to us and was not to them. The main point is not obscure: the day has not yet come, certain things must happen first, and Christ wins.

Eschatology for new converts. The sentence also tells us something about Paul’s teaching. He was in Thessalonica for a few weeks, perhaps a little longer (Acts 17:2; Philippians 4:16), working night and day (1 Thessalonians 2:9), with brand-new converts out of paganism, and in that time he taught them the sequence of the last things in enough detail to refer to it now in shorthand. Paul did not regard teaching about the last things as advanced material to be held back. When they later panicked, the remedy he reached for was: you already know this.

If some of Paul’s spoken teaching is lost, are we missing something we need? No. God has given us in Scripture everything necessary for his glory and our salvation, faith and life (the Westminster Confession 1.6; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.6). What Paul said aloud in Thessalonica on this subject helped them with details we cannot now recover, but nothing we need for faith and obedience was left out of what God caused to be written. The parts of this chapter that are dark to us are dark at the edges, not at the centre. Hold firmly what is clear, hold loosely what is uncertain, and do not let anyone fill the gap with a confident guess.

verseByVerse.quote: And you know what is restraining him now so that he may be revealed in his time. For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work. Only he who now restrains it will do so until he is out of the way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What is restraining him now. These are the two most argued-over verses in the letter, and honesty about what we do not know is the first requirement. Note a grammatical oddity any theory has to account for. In v. 6 the restrainer is neuter: to katechon, what restrains, the thing. In v. 7 it is masculine: ho katechōn, he who restrains, the person. Something and someone is holding back the man of lawlessness. Paul moves between a force and a person without explanation, because his readers knew what he meant (v. 5) and we do not.

Revealed in his time. In God’s appointed time, not before. The lawless one does not choose his own hour and cannot force it. Even the final rebellion runs on a timetable set by the one it is rebelling against. That is the pastoral point in a passage full of darkness, and it is why Paul can describe all this to a frightened church without leaving them frightened.

The mystery of lawlessness. Present tense, in the first century. What will finally appear in one figure is not dormant until then; it is operating now, underground. Mystery here means something hidden and not yet disclosed. Every age has seen it surface, and every age has seen it pushed back down.

Until he is out of the way. Whatever the restrainer is, the passage says plainly that evil is currently being held back. The world as we find it, bad as the news is, is not evil running at full strength. Someone has a hand on it.

Where Christians differ: who is the restrainer? No one now knows for certain what “restrains” the lawless one; the Thessalonians knew (v. 6), but we do not. Suggestions include: the Roman empire and the rule of law (the most common early church view); the Holy Spirit; the preaching of the gospel; the archangel Michael; or Paul himself. Some dispensationalists (Christians who read history as a series of distinct eras, with separate purposes for Israel and the church) argue that the restrainer is the Holy Spirit in the church, removed at a pre-tribulation rapture. Verdict: The best answer is humility: Paul does not tell us. Most likely he refers to God’s restraining providence, working through the order of government and law (Romans 13:1–4), which holds back the full outbreak of lawlessness until God permits it. Nothing in the passage teaches a secret rapture of the church; Paul never mentions believers being removed here, and the gathering to Christ comes with his visible coming (v. 1).

Weighing the proposals. Each has real support. The Roman state held anarchy back, and Paul calls the governing authority God’s servant (Romans 13:4); this would also explain why he writes so guardedly, since predicting the empire’s removal in writing was dangerous. The preaching of the gospel, which must go to all nations first (Matthew 24:14), is a serious suggestion. The angelic guardian Michael, who stands over God’s people in Daniel (Daniel 12:1), fits the masculine. Paul himself is the weakest candidate, since he died long ago and the restraint continues. And the Holy Spirit, as the restrainer who is removed, faces the problem that the Spirit is everywhere, and Scripture nowhere speaks of his being taken from the world.

All authority. Behind every candidate stands God, whose hand holds the restraint and who alone decides when to lift it: the God who has given all authority in heaven and on earth to his risen Son (Matthew 28:18). The governments that keep order are God’s servants under the rule of the exalted Christ, whether they know it or not. The church does not need to identify the restrainer to be at peace. It needs to know who sits above the restrainer: the same Lord Jesus who will end the lawless one with a breath (v. 8). Nor does God’s control make him the author of the evil he restrains. He holds it back, he judges it, and in the end his Son destroys it.

Does until he is out of the way mean the church will be taken away first? Dispensational Christians argue that the restrainer is the Spirit working through the church, so that when the church is raptured, the lawless one will be revealed. But Paul never says the restrainer is the church, the Spirit is everywhere and cannot leave the world, and the next verse says the lawless one is destroyed by the appearance of his coming (v. 8), the same coming at which believers are gathered (v. 1). The church is not the thing removed. It is the people who will see the lawless one appear and then see him fall.

If evil is being restrained, why is the world still so bad? Because what we see is sin under restraint, not sin at full strength, and that should frighten and comfort us at once. Every law that punishes violence, every court that convicts a thief, every conscience that flinches, every government that keeps a basic order, is part of God’s restraining mercy (Romans 13:3–4). Without it the world would be unlivable. The evil that breaks through is real and grievous, and God will judge it; but the fact that we can still live, work, marry, worship and raise children is a daily gift of a God who is holding back the flood.

On a Tuesday. Pray for those in authority this week by name: your national leaders, your local council, the police, the judges (1 Timothy 2:1–2). Their work, however imperfect, is one of the means by which God holds back lawlessness so that the gospel can be preached and his people can live quiet and peaceable lives.

For worship. The God who said to the sea, thus far shall you come, and no farther (Job 38:11), has drawn the same shoreline around the mystery of lawlessness. It works, but only within a fence he has set; it will be revealed, but only in his time; and when it is let out at last, it will be let out only to meet the Son who ends it with a breath. The whole history of evil is a leash in the hand of our Father, and the last day is kept for his Son.
verseByVerse.note: No one now knows for certain what “restrains” the lawless one; suggestions include the rule of law, the Roman empire, and the preaching of the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and bring to nothing by the appearance of his coming.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The breath of his mouth. After all that build-up, here is the confrontation, and it is over before it begins. There is no battle, no struggle, no uncertainty about the result. The Lord does not draw a sword; he exhales. The word is pneuma, breath, the same word as spirit and wind. Paul is quoting Isaiah, where the shoot from the stump of Jesse shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall kill the wicked (Isaiah 11:4). John sees the same thing: from the mouth of the rider on the white horse comes a sharp sword, and the enemies of God fall before it (Revelation 19:15, 21). The word that said let there be light, and the word that said Lazarus, come out, is the word that ends him.

The appearance of his coming. The second phrase does the same work. “Appearance” is epiphaneia: manifestation, shining forth, the word for a god’s visible appearing; and “coming” is parousia again. He brings him to nothing not by what he does on arriving but by arriving. The lawless one is undone the way darkness is undone when somebody opens a shutter, and the man who claimed to be God is undone by the true God’s appearing.

The proportions are the message. That deliberate anticlimax is the passage’s whole pastoral strategy. Paul has spent several verses making this figure as alarming as possible, and then disposes of him in half a sentence, with a breath. Whatever this power turns out to be, it is not in the same category as the one who ends it. Paul is not giving the church a monster to watch for. He is telling a shaken congregation that the worst thing coming will be dealt with by the Lord Jesus without effort.

Is this the same as the battle of Armageddon? It describes the same reality: the final overthrow of every power opposed to Christ at his return (Revelation 16:14–16; 19:11–21). But look at how both passages present it. Revelation’s battle has no fighting described; the armies gather and are struck down by the sword from Christ’s mouth. Paul’s version has only a breath. Scripture never pictures the end as a long war whose outcome is in doubt. It pictures a gathering of rebellion and then its instant collapse before the appearing of the King. That one event, the visible coming of Christ, brings the resurrection, the gathering of his people, the destruction of the lawless one and the final judgement together.

On a Tuesday. Think of the thing in the news or in your own life that most frightens you: a regime, an ideology, a disease, a person who has power over you. Put it in this verse. Whatever it is, it is smaller than the breath of Jesus. Pray about it with that size in mind.

For worship. The whole accumulated rebellion of history, given its moment and its champion, does not survive his appearing. One breath, one shining, and it is over. This is the King we serve: the Word through whom the worlds were made, whose speech is power, whose presence is light, and before whose face every claim to deity falls silent. Let the nations rage. He has only to come.
