verseByVerse.quote: The coming of the lawless one is by the activity of Satan with all power and false signs and wonders, and with all wicked deception for those who are perishing, because they refused to love the truth and so be saved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The activity of Satan. Note the word Paul chooses for his arrival: parousia, the royal-visit word he has used of Christ. The counterfeit runs all the way down, even to the vocabulary. The lawless one has a coming, a revealing, signs and wonders, and a claim to be God, and behind it all is the energeia, the working energy, of Satan. The devil has never created anything; he can only imitate and distort.

False signs and wonders. Power, signs and wonders: the standard biblical trio for God’s own mighty works. It is how Peter describes the ministry of Jesus at Pentecost, a man attested to you by God with mighty works and wonders and signs (Acts 2:22). The lawless one has the same list, here in counterfeit. And the adjective attached is false: literally, of the lie. Not that the phenomena are necessarily fake conjuring tricks, but that they are lies, signs pointing somewhere untrue. Miracles alone do not prove truth. Deuteronomy had already ruled on it: if a prophet gives a sign and it comes to pass, and then says let us go after other gods, do not listen, for the LORD is testing you (Deuteronomy 13:1–3). Jesus said the same, that false christs would perform great signs (Matthew 24:24), and John saw the beast’s prophet make fire come down from heaven (Revelation 13:13–14). The test of a message is never its power. It is its truth.

Wicked deception. Deception is his main weapon. He does not chiefly conquer by force but by persuasion: a lie dressed as light, a miracle in the service of falsehood. And it works on those who are perishing, who are already on the road to ruin.

They refused to love the truth. Then Paul explains why the deception works, in a searching sentence. He does not say they failed to grasp the truth, or were never given it, or found the arguments unconvincing. He says they refused to love it. The problem is located in the affections, not the intellect. Truth was available and they did not want it: not ignorance but a moral refusal to receive and love the gospel, which is not curable by better evidence. That is not a verdict anyone may pass on a particular doubter: honest questions are not the same as refusing to love the truth, and many who now believe once asked them. But most of us know this from the inside. We find it easiest to believe whatever lets us keep what we already love, whether comfort, control or the good opinion of the people around us, and hardest to believe the truth that would cost us them. And the little clause hanging on the end matters: and so be saved. Loving the truth was the road out. It was open. Paul does not present these people as trapped by circumstances beyond them; he presents them as having declined a rescue. That is what makes the next two verses bearable, and it is where they have to be read from.

How can I tell a true work of God from a false one? Not by how impressive it is, but by what it points to and whether it agrees with Scripture. Ask: does this exalt the Christ of the Bible, crucified and risen, as Lord? (1 John 4:1–3). Does the message match what the apostles taught, or add to it? (Galatians 1:8). Does it lead people to repentance, holiness and love, or to fascination with the spectacular and with the person doing it? A genuine answer to prayer, a healing, a providence, will always send you to Christ and his word. Anything that makes you need a new revelation, a special leader or a sign to believe is already leading you away.

Can a real Christian be deceived? A believer can be confused, misled for a time, or wrong on many things; the Thessalonians themselves were shaken by a false message. But a true believer will not finally be carried away into the lie of the lawless one, because God keeps his own and gives them a love for the truth that he does not let die (John 10:27–29). The way God keeps us is not by making deception impossible to meet, but by giving us his word, his Spirit and his church, and by making us love the truth. Stay close to all three.

On a Tuesday. Ask God for a love for the truth, and watch where truth costs you something: the passage you avoid because it rebukes you, the doctrine you resist because it humbles you, the fact about yourself you would rather not hear. Love for the truth is tested exactly there.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore God sends them a strong delusion, so that they may believe what is false, in order that all may be condemned who did not believe the truth but had pleasure in unrighteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A strong delusion. This is one of the hardest sentences in Paul, and it should not be softened. God is the subject of the verb. “Strong delusion” is energeia planēs: a working of error, an active power of deception. Everything depends on therefore: this is not God’s opening move. It follows v. 10: because they refused to love the truth. The delusion is a judicial response to a prior refusal, not an arbitrary act on a neutral party. God confirms the blindness they chose.

The old pattern. It is what happened to Pharaoh, who hardened his own heart, and whose heart God hardened (Exodus 8:15; 9:12). It is the lying spirit God permitted to deceive Ahab’s prophets, after Ahab had spent his life refusing the true word (1 Kings 22:19–23). It is Romans 1, where three times God gave them up to what they had already chosen (Romans 1:24–28). In each case God stops obstructing a person’s own direction of travel and lets them have what they insisted on. There is a terrible mercy in the restraint that precedes it, and a terrible justice in its removal.

What is false. Literally, the lie: the great lie of the lawless one, that he is God. It is the lie of the garden in its final form, and people who would not have the truth are given the lie they preferred.

Had pleasure in unrighteousness. Verse 12 states the outcome and repeats the ground. They did not merely disbelieve; they enjoyed the alternative. Unbelief is often moral before it is intellectual: the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil (John 3:19–20).

The truth has a face. The truth they did not believe is not a set of ideas floating free. It is the gospel of 1:8, and at its centre a Person, who said, I am the way, and the truth, and the life (John 14:6). The light they hated was the Son himself, the true light coming into the world (John 1:9). So the final delusion is the end of a long refusal of Christ. And the lie they come to believe, that a man may make himself God, is the exact inversion of the truth they rejected, that God became man to save sinners. Those who would not have the Son who humbled himself are given over to the man who exalts himself.

Where Christians differ: does God cause people to believe lies? Some find this incompatible with God’s goodness. Verdict: God is not the author of sin, and he does not deceive the innocent. He sends delusion as a judgement on those who have already refused the truth and loved unrighteousness, giving them over to what they chose. Like the hardening of Pharaoh, it confirms and punishes persistent rebellion (the Westminster Confession 5.6; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 5.6). The sinner remains fully responsible.

Could this describe me? I am afraid I am deluded. Anyone anxious that this describes them has, by that anxiety, given the evidence against it. The mark of the people in these verses is that they do not want the truth and are content. Wanting it is the opposite condition, and it is the beginning of the road out that v. 10 says was open. This passage has never been given to anyone as a diagnosis of their neighbours, nor as a weapon for tender consciences. It was written to comfort a church that was wondering how so many could be taken in, and the answer is that God is not absent even from that, and the outcome is not in doubt. If you want Christ, come to him; he has promised never to cast out anyone who comes (John 6:37).

On a Tuesday. Do not toy with sin. The road to blindness is gradual: a sin enjoyed, then excused, then defended, then a doctrine adjusted to make room for it. Watch whether you have begun reading the Bible to find permission rather than direction. If there is a sin you are enjoying, bring it into the light today, where Christ is faithful to forgive (1 John 1:9), before your mind builds arguments for it. But if there is a sin you hate and keep falling into, you are not the person these verses describe. A sin can be loved and hated at once, and the fight against it is itself the Spirit’s work in you (Romans 7:22–25; Galatians 5:17).

For worship. God is just in every judgement, and nothing he sends is unfair. But the same God who gives the persistent rebel over to the lie he chose has, for countless others, refused to give them over. He pursued us in his Son when we too loved the darkness, broke through our preferences, and gave us a love for the truth we did not have. That we see at all is mercy. That we love Christ at all is grace. The difference between the deluded and the saved is not that we were wiser, but that he was kind.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Against that darkness Paul sets God’s choice of the Thessalonians and his call through the gospel, then asks them to stand firm in what they were taught, and prays for their hearts (vv. 13–17).
verseByVerse.theology:
Election, and the Means It Arrives By

Verse 13 compresses the whole of salvation into one Trinitarian sentence: God chose, the Spirit sanctified, they believed, and glory lies ahead — and verse 14 refuses to let election float free of the means: it reached them ‘through our gospel’.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: After the lawless one and the delusion, what Paul asks for is undramatic: stand firm and hold to what you were taught.

Now: Teaching about the last things is meant to produce steadiness in ‘every good work and word’ (v. 17).

verseByVerse.quote: But we ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers beloved by the Lord, because God chose you as the firstfruits to be saved, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth. To this he called you through our gospel, so that you may obtain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers beloved by the Lord. A sharp reversal. From people who refused the truth and stand condemned, he turns to the congregation, and the contrast is total, point for point. They refused to love the truth; these were chosen. They were given a delusion; these were sanctified by the Spirit. They had pleasure in unrighteousness; these believed the truth. In the first letter he called them loved by God (1 Thessalonians 1:4); here the love is Christ’s.

God chose you. Here is the compressed statement of salvation, and it is Trinitarian in one sentence. Father, Spirit, Son: choosing, sanctifying, and the glory they are travelling toward. “Chose you as the firstfruits” involves a genuine textual question. The Greek manuscripts divide between aparchēn, firstfruits, and ap’ archēs, from the beginning, and the two look almost identical in the uncial script. Some manuscripts, followed by the KJV and NKJV, read chose you from the beginning, as the ESV notes: from eternity. Firstfruits would mean among the first converts in their city and region, the first sheaf of a harvest God would go on reaping. Either way, election: the initiative was God’s and it came first. Election is God choosing, before the foundation of the world, particular people to be his own and to be saved, moved by his love and by nothing he found in them (Ephesians 1:4–5). The difference does not affect the doctrine.

Sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth. Sanctification here is the Spirit’s work of claiming a person for God: setting him apart at conversion, and then making him holy in practice for the rest of his life (1 Thessalonians 4:3; 5:23). God chose the end (salvation) and the means (the Spirit’s work and faith): no one is saved without trusting Christ, and no one who trusts him need wonder whether God chose him.

Through our gospel. Verse 14 anchors it to something they can remember. Election was worked out in history through the preaching of the gospel and the effectual call, that is, God’s inward summons by which the outward message actually brings a person to Christ (1 Corinthians 1:23–24). The eternal choice reached them through three men preaching in their town. Paul never lets election float free of the means: it arrived by way of a sermon somebody actually delivered, which is exactly the point he made at 1:10 about the testimony that was believed.

The glory of our Lord Jesus Christ. The goal: sharing Christ’s glory. It is the pattern of Romans 8:30, the chain that runs from God’s choosing to glory: chosen, called, sanctified, believing, glorified. And set it beside v. 4, where the lawless one grabs at the place of God. The thing the usurper tries to seize is given away freely to a persecuted congregation in Macedonia.

What kind of election is this? Arminian Christians, brothers who also confess salvation by grace, hold that God chose those he foresaw would believe. But Paul says God chose them to be saved, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth: faith and holiness are the means God chose to bring them to salvation, not the reason he chose them. The cause of the choice lies in God, in his love, not in anything foreseen in them.

How can I know I am chosen? Not by looking into God’s secret decree, but by what God has done. Look at the chain Paul gives: called through the gospel, believing the truth, being made holy by the Spirit. If you have believed the truth and the Spirit is making you holy, you have the marks of God’s choice. You do not climb into heaven to read the book of life; you look at Christ, trust him, and see the fruit he is producing. Election is not a riddle to be solved before you dare to believe. It is a comfort given to those who already believe, to tell them their faith was God’s idea before it was theirs.

If God has chosen, why should we evangelise? Because God chose the means as well as the end. He chose these people to be saved through belief in the truth, and he called them through our gospel. No one believes without hearing, and no one hears without a preacher (Romans 10:14). Election is the reason evangelism succeeds, not the reason to stop. Paul endured everything for the sake of the elect, that they might obtain salvation (2 Timothy 2:10). We do not know who they are; we preach to everyone, and God brings his own.

In a sentence. Against all the darkness of the last days stands the Father’s choice, the Spirit’s sanctifying, the gospel’s call and the glory of Christ at the end, and none of it depends on us.

verseByVerse.quote: So then, brothers, stand firm and hold to the traditions that you were taught by us, either by our spoken word or by our letter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stand firm. So then points back to vv. 13–14: because God chose, called and will glorify them, this is what Paul asks them to do, and neither verb is dramatic. “Stand firm” is stēkete, the soldier holding his position, the same word Paul used in the first letter (1 Thessalonians 3:8). Not advance, not counter-attack, not work out the timetable. Hold the ground you are on, where the sanctifying Spirit of v. 13 has set you.

Hold to the traditions. “Hold” is krateite: grip, keep hold of. And paradoseis, traditions, means simply what has been handed over: a deposit passed from one person to the next. Here it means the apostolic teaching handed on to them, not later church customs.

Spoken word or letter. Paul puts his preaching and his writing on the same level. What he said in their house and what he sent by courier are the same deposit in two forms. It is one of the earliest indications that apostolic writing was regarded as carrying the weight of apostolic speech. The spoken half we no longer have (v. 5); the written half is what we are reading.

Where Christians differ: Scripture and tradition. The Roman Catholic Church cites this verse to argue that there are two sources of authority: Scripture and unwritten apostolic tradition passed down through the church. Orthodox churches hold a similar view, and both honour the apostles’ teaching deeply. Verdict: Paul’s oral and written teaching had equal authority, because both came from the apostle. But the content of the apostolic tradition is now preserved for us in the written Scriptures. We have no reliable access to other apostolic oral teaching beyond what is written. The apostles’ spoken teaching was the same gospel they wrote down, and Paul himself points the church to what we say in this letter (3:14). So Scripture alone is now the final and sufficient rule of faith, by which all later traditions must be tested (the Westminster Confession 1.6, 10; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.6, 10; 2 Timothy 3:16–17).

The answer to the crisis. They had been shaken by a spirit, a word, or a letter claiming to be his (v. 2). The remedy is not a new revelation to settle the matter, and not a better prophet. It is: go back to what you were actually taught, and hold on. A congregation that knows what it was given is very hard to panic.

What was handed over. The traditions have a centre, and Paul names it when he lists what he delivered as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Holding to the traditions is holding to him. Paul can even say that the Colossians received Christ Jesus the Lord, as one receives a tradition, and warn them against teaching according to human tradition and not according to Christ (Colossians 2:6–8). That is the line between the apostolic deposit and every later addition: the one hands on Christ, the other hands on men. To stand firm is to keep hold of the Lord who was handed to us.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all tradition is bad. Creeds and confessions are valuable when they faithfully summarise Scripture. The Apostles’ Creed, the Nicene Creed, and the great Reformation confessions are handed-on treasure, and wise Christians read them gladly. But they stand under Scripture, and are to be corrected by it.

What does holding to the traditions look like in practice? It means knowing what the apostles taught well enough to recognise when someone departs from it. Read the New Testament regularly and whole, not only in fragments. Learn a good summary of the faith, a catechism or confession, so that the shape of the gospel is fixed in your mind. Sit under preaching that explains the text. And when a new teaching arrives, however exciting or however authoritative the speaker, ask where it is written. Holding on is not a feeling of conviction; it is a habit of returning, again and again, to the word that was handed to you.
verseByVerse.note: “Traditions” here means the apostolic teaching handed on to them, whether in person or in writing.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and gave us eternal comfort and good hope through grace, comfort your hearts and establish them in every good work and word.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father. The chapter that has contained the darkest material in the letter ends in prayer, and the grammar is the same quiet marvel as in the first letter. Christ is named first here, then the Father: an equal place. It would be an odd thing to write if he thought the two were on different sides of the line between Creator and creature. And the verbs that follow (comfort, establish) are singular, as in 1 Thessalonians 3:11: two subjects, one action. It is not a doctrine being argued but the ordinary shape of his praying.

Who loved us. Three things said about God, all in the past tense, before anything is asked: a decisive act of love, at the cross. The request in v. 17 rests entirely on what has already been done. Paul does not ask God to start loving them; he asks him to continue in a direction already established. “Eternal comfort” is a striking pairing: encouragement that never runs out. Their comfort in the present had been badly shaken; that is the whole occasion of the letter. Paul tells them the comfort they have been given is of a kind that outlasts the thing shaking it. And good hope is not a wish but a sure expectation of glory, all through grace.

Comfort your hearts and establish them. Comfort (parakaleō) means coming alongside to strengthen, not merely to soothe. “Establish” (stērizō) is the buttressing word, to prop what is leaning. It is the very thing Timothy had been sent to do in the first letter (1 Thessalonians 3:2). And note where it lands: in every good work and word. Not in correct opinions about the end times, which is what the chapter has been about, but in what they do and what they say. Paul has just spent most of twelve verses on the man of lawlessness, and the outcome he prays for is a congregation whose deeds and speech are steady. That is a fair measure of what the doctrine of the last things is for.

What if I do not feel comforted? Paul’s prayer assumes the comfort has already been given (gave us eternal comfort) and asks that it would reach their hearts. The gift and the feeling of it are not the same. Your comfort rests on facts: God loved you, Christ died for you, your hope is secured by grace. Feelings follow facts slowly, and sometimes only after a long night. So do what Paul did: pray for it. Ask the Father and the Son to comfort your heart, rehearse what they have done, and keep doing the next good work and speaking the next good word while you wait. The steadiness often comes in the doing.

On a Tuesday. Pray this blessing for someone who is anxious about the future: a teenager frightened by the news, an older believer facing death, a friend shaken by a loud prophecy. Pray it over them by name, and then send them a message with these two verses in it.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>Now concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our being gathered together to him, we ask you, brothers,<sup>2</sup>not to be quickly shaken in mind or alarmed, either by a spirit or a spoken word, or a letter seeming to be from us, to the effect that the day of the Lord has come.<sup>3</sup>Let no one deceive you in any way. For that day will not come, unless the rebellion comes first, and the man of lawlessness is revealed, the son of destruction,<sup>4</sup>who opposes and exalts himself against every so-called god or object of worship, so that he takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God.<sup>5</sup>Do you not remember that when I was still with you I told you these things?<sup>6</sup>And you know what is restraining him now so that he may be revealed in his time.<sup>7</sup>For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work. Only he who now restrains it will do so until he is out of the way.<sup>8</sup>And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and bring to nothing by the appearance of his coming.<sup>9</sup>The coming of the lawless one is by the activity of Satan with all power and false signs and wonders,<sup>10</sup>and with all wicked deception for those who are perishing, because they refused to love the truth and so be saved.<sup>11</sup>Therefore God sends them a strong delusion, so that they may believe what is false,<sup>12</sup>in order that all may be condemned who did not believe the truth but had pleasure in unrighteousness.<sup>13</sup>But we ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers beloved by the Lord, because God chose you as the firstfruits to be saved, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth.<sup>14</sup>To this he called you through our gospel, so that you may obtain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.<sup>15</sup>So then, brothers, stand firm and hold to the traditions that you were taught by us, either by our spoken word or by our letter.<sup>16</sup>Now may our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and gave us eternal comfort and good hope through grace,<sup>17</sup>comfort your hearts and establish them in every good work and word.

3.title: The Lord Is Faithful
3.overview:
Paul asks for prayer that the word of the Lord will run ahead, and assures them that the Lord is faithful and will guard them. Then he deals firmly with a problem that has grown since his first letter: some believers, probably excited about Christ’s return, have stopped working and are living off others while meddling in everyone’s business. Paul had worked night and day to support himself as an example, and had taught them, “If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat.”

The church must withdraw ordinary support and fellowship from such people, yet treat them as brothers, not enemies. The letter ends with peace, Paul’s own signature against forgery, and grace for all.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A request for prayer, a promise of the Lord’s faithfulness, and a prayer for their hearts, before the hard commands that follow (vv. 1–5).
verseByVerse.theology:
Faithless, and Faithful

‘Not all have faith’, ‘but the Lord is faithful’ (vv. 2–3): Paul answers human faithlessness not with a better estimate of people but with a reliable Lord, who promises not exemption from trouble but to establish and guard his people through it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul wrote from Corinth, where Acts 18 records exactly the ‘wicked and evil men’ of verse 2.

Now: Confidence placed ‘in the Lord about you’ (v. 4) survives disappointment, because it never rested on the people themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, brothers, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may speed ahead and be honored, as happened among you, and that we may be delivered from wicked and evil men. For not all have faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 2 Thessalonians 3 turns from the great events of the end to the ordinary life of a church waiting for them. First, prayer and confidence: pray that the gospel will run and that Paul will be rescued from hostile men; the Lord is faithful and will guard them from the evil one (vv. 1–5). Second, discipline: some had stopped working and were living off others and meddling. Paul commands the church to keep away from them, points to his own example, repeats his rule that whoever will not work should not eat, and tells the church to warn the disobedient as brothers, not enemies (vv. 6–15). Third, a prayer for peace, his own signature against forgeries, and grace (vv. 16–18). A right hope of Christ’s coming does not make people idle; it makes them faithful, busy and orderly.

The setting. In 1 Thessalonians Paul had already told the church to work with their hands and live quietly (1 Thessalonians 4:11–12) and to warn the idle (1 Thessalonians 5:14). The problem had grown. The false report that the day of the Lord had already come (2:2) may have fed it: if the end is here, why go on working? Or the idle may simply have been taking advantage of the generosity of richer believers, as clients in Greek and Roman cities lived off patrons. Either way, Paul treats it as a matter of obedience to the apostolic tradition, not merely of manners.

Pray for us. “Finally” (to loipon, as for the rest) marks the move to the closing section, not the very last word. “Pray” is present tense: keep praying. The apostle who has just written about the man of lawlessness, and who prays for them (1:11), asks a harassed provincial congregation to pray for him, as he does in letter after letter. Prayer runs both ways in the body of Christ; no minister is above needing the prayers of his people.

Speed ahead. Look at what he asks for. Not safety, not release, not success, but the progress of the message. The verb (trechē) is literally run, and Paul is probably echoing Psalm 147:15, where God’s word runs swiftly. The picture is of a herald who cannot be overtaken. He asks for the message to move, not for the messenger to be comfortable. And the word is of the Lord: it is Christ’s word, carried by Paul.

As happened among you. “Be honoured” (doxazētai) means be glorified: the same thing he prayed for in 1:12. The word is glorified when people receive it as God’s word and their lives are changed by it, rather than merely hearing and shelving it. Then the gracious clause: he holds up their own conversion as the pattern of what he is asking God to do elsewhere (1 Thessalonians 1:5–6; 2:13). Frightened, confused and harbouring a group who had stopped working, they are still his example of the gospel running well. He was probably writing from Corinth, and he wanted Corinth to become what Thessalonica had become.

Wicked and evil men. The second request is more personal. “Delivered” (rhysthōmen) means rescued. “Wicked” (atopos) is literally out of place: perverse, unreasonable, people with whom argument does not work. “Evil” (ponēros) is actively malicious. The definite article in Greek suggests particular opponents, probably those in Corinth who opposed Paul. Acts 18 records just such opposition: a united attack, Paul dragged before the proconsul Gallio (Acts 18:5–17).

I have many in this city. During that stay in Corinth the Lord himself spoke to Paul one night in a vision: Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many in this city who are my people (Acts 18:9–10). That is why the word runs. The risen Christ is running it. He had people in Corinth not yet converted whom he already called his own, and the opposition of wicked men could not keep his voice from reaching them. Paul asks the church to pray for what the Lord of the harvest has already determined to do, and their prayers become part of how he does it.

Not all have faith. Literally, for not of all is the faith. A short sentence, almost an understatement, and it is Paul’s explanation for opposition. He does not attribute hostility to misunderstanding, or assume better presentation would resolve it. Some people do not believe, and their not believing has consequences for those who do. Nor is faith something all people could produce if only they tried harder; it is God’s gift (Ephesians 2:8; Philippians 1:29), which is why Paul prays. The sentence also prepares for v. 3 by contrast: people are unfaithful, but the Lord is faithful.

If God is sovereign, does my prayer actually change anything? Yes, because God has chosen to work through it. He decreed not only the ends but the means, and the prayers of his people are among the means (James 5:16). Paul did not think the gospel would run whether or not the Thessalonians prayed; he asked them because he believed their prayers would be part of how God made it run. Sovereignty is not a reason to stop praying; it is the reason prayer is worth anything. You are not asking a God who might be unable, but a God who is able and who delights to answer.

When I meet hostility for sharing my faith, have I done it wrong? Not necessarily. Paul met it constantly, and he was not tactless; he simply said, for not all have faith. Sometimes we do handle things badly, and we should be humble enough to ask (Colossians 4:5–6; 1 Peter 3:15–16). But the gospel itself offends, and the most gracious witness in history was crucified. Knowing this in advance prevents a Christian from concluding, every time he meets real opposition, that he must have failed. Be gentle, be clear, and leave the result with God.

On a Tuesday. Pray this week for one missionary or minister by name: that the word would run through their work, and that they would be protected from those who oppose it. Ask them what to pray for, and then tell them you did.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Lord is faithful. He will establish you and guard you against the evil one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord is faithful. Read it directly after v. 2 and you will hear the wordplay: not all have faith (pistis), but faithful (pistos) is the Lord. Human faithlessness is real; the sentence that answers it is not about better people but about a reliable Lord, and faithful stands first for emphasis. “The Lord” here is Christ, as usually in these letters. His faithfulness means he keeps his promises and finishes what he begins: he who calls you is faithful, and he will surely do it (1 Thessalonians 5:24; 1 Corinthians 1:9; Philippians 1:6).

He will establish you. “Establish” (stērixei) means make firm, set fast: the buttressing word, to prop what is leaning. It is the fourth time it has appeared in the Thessalonian correspondence: Timothy was sent to establish them (1 Thessalonians 3:2), Paul prayed God would establish their hearts (1 Thessalonians 3:13; 2 Thessalonians 2:17), and now he states it as a promise. They had been shaken (2:2), and the promise is aimed exactly at that.

Guard you against the evil one. “Guard” (phylaxei) is a sentry’s word: to keep watch over, protect, like a garrison, a picture close to Philippians 4:7. “The evil one” could grammatically mean evil in general, but here, after chapter 2’s talk of Satan’s activity (2:9), it almost certainly means Satan himself, as many read the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:13) and Jesus’ prayer for his disciples (John 17:15). It is the petition of the Lord’s Prayer, answered as a statement. Satan wants to shake believers loose, by persecution, by false teaching, or by disorder in the church. Christ guards his own.

In it with them. Paul asks for prayer and gives reassurance in the same breath, the mark of someone genuinely in it with the people he is writing to. And there is a quiet realism here. Paul does not promise they will be spared trouble; he has just spent a chapter and a half saying they will not be. He promises they will be held and guarded through it. That is a different assurance, and it is the one Scripture gives again and again.

Where Christians differ: can a true believer finally fall away? Arminian traditions (which hold that God’s saving grace can finally be resisted) and some Lutheran traditions teach that a genuine believer may lose salvation by turning away; they press the Bible’s warnings seriously, and their concern for holy living is one to share. Verdict: Verses like this one ground the Reformed doctrine of perseverance. The promise rests not on our grip on Christ but on his faithfulness: “he will establish you and guard you.” Those whom God has chosen and called (2:13–14) he keeps to the end (John 10:28–29; Romans 8:30; 1 Peter 1:5). This does not make warnings pointless; the warnings are among the means by which he keeps us. And those who finally fall away show that they were never truly his (1 John 2:19).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers will never be attacked or never stumble. Satan does attack, and believers do sin; the Lord will not let the evil one finally destroy their faith. Nor does it make us passive: Paul still commands them (v. 4) and prays for them (v. 5). And a believer afraid that he might fall away may take this verse as written to him: his safety rests on the Lord’s faithfulness, not on the strength of his fears.

What does an attack of the evil one look like in an ordinary Christian life? Rarely anything dramatic. More often it is an accusation that will not let you rest in forgiveness (Revelation 12:10), a doubt pressed at a weak moment, a temptation timed to your tiredness, a quarrel stirred in the church, or a lie about God’s goodness whispered in suffering. Scripture tells us to resist him, firm in the faith (1 Peter 5:8–9), and to put on the armour God supplies: truth, righteousness, the gospel, faith, the word, and prayer (Ephesians 6:10–18). You do not fight alone. The Lord who guards you has already defeated him at the cross (Colossians 2:15).

On a Tuesday. Think of the point at which you feel most likely to give way: a habit, a fear, a relationship, a doubt. Bring that exact point to Christ in prayer and ask him to set a guard there. Your security is not your watchfulness, though you must watch; it is his.

For worship. People fail, churches fail, and our own hearts fail us daily, but the Lord is faithful. When Satan demanded to sift Simon like wheat, Jesus had already prayed for him that his faith would not fail (Luke 22:31–32); and Peter fell, and was not lost. The same Lord stands sentry over his people in the dark and intercedes for them still. The faithful Lord’s grip does not depend on ours.

verseByVerse.quote: And we have confidence in the Lord about you, that you are doing and will do the things that we command. May the Lord direct your hearts to the love of God and to the steadfastness of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Confidence in the Lord. The verb (pepoithamen, perfect tense) means we have been persuaded and remain so. Paul is about to issue some hard instructions, and he expresses trust before giving correction. But look where the confidence is placed: in the Lord about you. Not in their natural goodness or their track record, which had already wobbled. Because the Lord is at work in them (v. 3), Paul can trust that they will obey. That is a form of confidence that survives disappointment, because it was never resting on the person in the first place.

The things that we command. “Command” (parangellō) means give orders, charge: a military and legal word. It appears four times in this chapter. Paul speaks with apostolic authority: his instructions are not suggestions but the Lord’s commands through his apostle (1 Thessalonians 4:2).

May the Lord direct your hearts. “Direct” (kateuthynai) means make straight, clear a road. It is the same verb he used in 1 Thessalonians 3:11, asking God to clear the way to Thessalonica. There it was a journey; here it is the heart. The affections need a road made through them as much as a traveller does. Obedience begins in the heart, and only the Lord can steer the heart: the king’s heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD (Proverbs 21:1).

To the love of God. Grammatically this could be our love for God or God’s love for us. Most likely Paul means God’s love for us: may the Lord lead you deeper into the experience and knowledge of God’s love (Romans 5:5; Ephesians 3:19), from which our love for God flows. You learn to love God by being brought into his love for you.

The steadfastness of Christ. “Steadfastness” (hypomonē) is patient endurance, bearing up under a load. It could be Christ’s own endurance, which they are to see and share (Hebrews 12:2–3), or the endurance that Christ gives. Probably both: the patient endurance that Christ showed under suffering, which he now works in his people as they wait for his return. This is the right response to chapter 2: not feverish excitement, but steady endurance. They needed staying power, and Paul does not tell them to find more of it. He asks God to point their hearts at a man who kept going all the way to a Roman cross. Steadfastness is not manufactured by resolution. It is drawn from somebody who has already done it.

In the flow. Verses 4 and 5 form a bridge between the promise that the Lord is faithful (vv. 1–3) and the hardest commands in the letter, about the idle (vv. 6–15). Paul crosses from one to the other by resting his confidence in the Lord rather than in the church, and by praying for their hearts before he addresses their habits.

How does the Lord direct my heart into his love in practice? Usually through ordinary means, used slowly. He sets his love before you in his word, especially at the cross (Romans 5:8; 1 John 4:10). He pours it into your heart by the Spirit (Romans 5:5). He shows it in the Lord’s Supper, in the fellowship of his people, and in providences you can trace afterwards. So put yourself where the road is being cleared: read of his love, meditate on it, sing it, and pray this verse. When your heart drifts toward fear, resentment or self-pity, ask him to turn it back, and then look again at Christ.

On a Tuesday. Before you correct anyone this week, a child, a colleague, a fellow believer, first tell them honestly what you are confident of in them, and where that confidence rests. Then speak.

verseByVerse.ref: 3:6–15 – Idleness, and How to Deal With It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The hardest section of the letter: what the church is to do with members who will not work. Paul gives the command, his own example, the rule, a word to the faithful, and the limits of discipline (vv. 6–15).
verseByVerse.theology:
Discipline That Aims at Restoration

Verses 14 and 15 must be held together: the withdrawal is real, its aim is the offender's own recovery, and he is still to be warned as a brother.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul could command the idle to work because he had worked night and day in front of them, declining support he had every right to (vv. 7–9).

Now: Verse 10 is about the unwilling, not the unable, and it governs the church's own table.

verseByVerse.quote: Now we command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you keep away from any brother who is walking in idleness and not in accord with the tradition that you received from us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the name of our Lord. The tone changes sharply. In the first letter Paul asked and urged (1 Thessalonians 4:1); here he commands, and does it under the highest authority available. Something has hardened since he last wrote. “In the name of” means by Christ’s authority and as his representative: not advice but a binding instruction. When Jesus first gave his church authority to deal with a sinning brother, he promised that where two or three are gathered in his name, there he is among them (Matthew 18:15–20). The setting of that promise is church discipline. The Lord himself stands behind a church that acts in his name, and he is the one doing the correcting.

Keep away. The verb (stellesthai) means draw back, hold aloof: Paul uses it of taking care to avoid blame over the collection (2 Corinthians 8:20). It is not excommunication: v. 15 will insist he is still a brother to be warned. What is being withdrawn is the ordinary support and easy fellowship that had been enabling the behaviour. If the community keeps feeding a man who will not work, the community is paying him to stay as he is.

Walking in idleness. “In idleness” (ataktōs) means disorderly, out of line. In use it described soldiers breaking ranks, and in everyday papyri apprentices skipping work; it is the word of 1 Thessalonians 5:14. In context (vv. 7–12) the specific disorder is refusing to work and living off others. “Walking” is the Bible’s word for a settled way of life, not a single slip. This is not about outsiders or the poor, but about members who had stopped working.

Not in accord with the tradition. “Tradition” (paradosis, what is handed down) is the same word as in 2:15. The apostolic tradition included not only doctrine but how to live, including the duty to work (1 Thessalonians 4:11–12), and it is now found in the New Testament. The problem is not that these people are irritating but that they contradict apostolic teaching by how they live. Paul treats a lifestyle as capable of being out of accord with the deposit, exactly as a doctrine can be.

Setting and background. Besides the excitement about the day and the habits of patronage (see the setting above), a third cause may have been a misunderstanding of Christian love, assuming the church owed them support. Paul’s answer covers all three: work is part of faithful waiting, love does not mean being a burden, and the church must not enable idleness.

Where Christians differ: how should church discipline be practised? Some churches practise almost no formal discipline; others make it harsh and quick. Verdict: Scripture requires real discipline, carried out by the church under its elders, aimed at restoring the sinner (Matthew 18:15–17; 1 Corinthians 5; Galatians 6:1). This passage describes a step short of full exclusion: the person is still a brother (v. 15), but the church withdraws close fellowship to bring him to shame and repentance. Discipline is graded to the offence and persistence, and it is always done in love, never as revenge.

Costly, not bureaucratic. This is a hard instruction, given to a small congregation where everyone knew everyone. Paul is telling people to change how they behave toward someone they will see next week, which is far more costly than any formal process, and is the only reason it could work.

What it does not mean. It does not mean shunning those who cannot work because of illness, disability, age, or lack of jobs. The issue is those who will not work (v. 10). Scripture repeatedly commands care for the genuinely needy (Galatians 2:10; 1 Timothy 5:3–16). Nor does it mean cutting off all contact; v. 15 says to warn him, which requires speaking.

What if the person living off others is my own adult child? The principle still applies, with the tenderness of a parent. Love wants the child to flourish, and flourishing includes the dignity of responsibility. Continuing to fund a settled refusal to work, when they are able, is not kindness; it is paying them to stay where they are. That does not mean throwing them out overnight or withdrawing love. It means talking honestly, setting clear expectations and a reasonable timeline, helping them toward work, and being willing to let them feel the consequences of refusing. If there is illness, depression or addiction behind it, get help for that; it is a different situation. Pray, keep speaking, and keep the door of the heart open.

On a Tuesday. Ask honestly: does your church’s kindness ever enable someone’s settled refusal to take responsibility? And ask the same of yourself: is there a responsibility God has given you that you have left others to carry? If so, there is forgiveness for that too, and the Spirit gives strength to take it up again.
verseByVerse.note: The problem of idleness in the church is now worse than when Paul wrote the first letter.

verseByVerse.quote: For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, because we were not idle when we were with you, nor did we eat anyone's bread without paying for it, but with toil and labor we worked night and day, that we might not be a burden to any of you. It was not because we do not have that right, but to give you in ourselves an example to imitate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Imitate us. Before pressing the command, Paul points at himself. “Imitate” (mimeisthai) means follow as an example; our word mimic comes from it. Doctrine was taught by word and shown by life, and “you ought” (dei, it is necessary) makes this imitation a duty.

We were not idle. The verb (ouk ētaktēsamen, we did not break ranks) is the verb form of the word in v. 6.

Anyone’s bread. “Eat bread” is a Hebrew way of saying get one’s living (Genesis 3:19; Amos 7:12). “Without paying” (dōrean) means as a gift, free. Paul did not live on anyone’s charity while in Thessalonica, though the Philippians sent him gifts there more than once (Philippians 4:16).

Toil and labor. It is almost word for word what he wrote in the first letter (1 Thessalonians 2:9): the workbench (probably a leatherworker’s), the double shift, the refusal to be carried. Two words are stacked: “toil” (kopos), labour to exhaustion, and “labour” (mochthos), hardship, the grind. Paul is not describing a trade he enjoyed but being tired. He was a tentmaker (Acts 18:3), and he worked long hours while also preaching and teaching.

Imitators of us and of the Lord. The chain of imitation does not stop at Paul. In the first letter he said they had become imitators of us and of the Lord (1 Thessalonians 1:6), and he told the Corinthians, be imitators of me, as I am of Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1). Paul’s bench in Thessalonica copied a bench in Nazareth. Jesus was known in his own town simply as the carpenter (Mark 6:3): the Lord of glory earned his bread with his hands through the long hidden years before his public ministry began. An apostle who would not be carried was following a Saviour who did not count ordinary work beneath him, and the idle in Thessalonica were being asked to follow the same Lord.

Not to weigh on any of you. The verb (epibarēsai) means weigh down. Paul did not want his support to fall on a young, poor and persecuted church, and he did not want anyone to say he preached for money (1 Thessalonians 2:5–6; 2 Corinthians 11:7–9).

That right. This is the sentence that keeps the passage from becoming a rule about ministers never being paid. “Right” (exousia) is authority, entitlement. Paul firmly taught that those who preach the gospel have the right to be supported by it: the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:4–14; Galatians 6:6; 1 Timothy 5:17–18; Luke 10:7). He gave up this right voluntarily, here, for a specific reason.

An example to imitate. “Example” (typos) is a pattern, a model (the word first meant the impression left by a stamp or die): the same word he used of the Thessalonians themselves (1 Thessalonians 1:7). Paul deliberately made himself a living pattern of honest work, going without money he was entitled to, so that no one could excuse idleness by appeal to spirituality. And that is what makes the command of v. 6 possible at all. When he tells the idle to work, every person reading the letter knows he has already done it in front of them.

Is my ordinary job really service to Christ? Yes, if it is lawful work done in faith. Paul’s leatherwork was part of his ministry, not a distraction from it, because it adorned the gospel and served his neighbours. The Reformers recovered this: the farmer, the nurse, the mother, the accountant, the cleaner all have a calling from God, not merely the minister. Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, for you are serving the Lord Christ (Colossians 3:23–24). Your diligence, honesty and cheerfulness at work are worship, and they preach to colleagues who will never enter a church.

On a Tuesday. The Lord who worked at a bench in Nazareth now works in you by his Spirit. Someone is watching how a Christian works: whether you arrive on time, whether you finish what you start, whether you complain, whether you cut corners when no one checks. And if you lead others, in a family, a team or a church, ask whether you are asking them to do anything you are not doing yourself.

verseByVerse.quote: For even when we were with you, we would give you this command: If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We would give you this command. The imperfect tense: we kept giving it. This was not a new rule invented for the crisis but standing instruction to new converts from the beginning. It belongs with the pattern of vv. 7–9: he had told them and he had shown them.

If anyone is not willing to work. It is among the best-known sentences Paul wrote and among the most abused, so the qualification in the middle of it has to be seen. The key word is “willing” (thelei, wants, chooses). The rule targets those who refuse to work, not those who are unable: a choice of the will, not misfortune. It is not about anyone who cannot find work, cannot do work, or cannot get enough of it. Paul is addressing people who had chosen idleness, perhaps for what they took to be spiritual reasons, and who were eating at the expense of a poor congregation while they did it.

Let him not eat. A command (third-person imperative), not merely a prediction. The church was not to feed those who could work but would not. The same principle runs through the book of Proverbs (Proverbs 10:4; 19:15; 20:4), and it reaches back to creation: humanity was made to work (Genesis 2:15), and after the fall work became toil but remained a calling (Genesis 3:19). God himself worked six days and rested; work is part of the image of a working God.

Bread that is worked for. Jesus met a version of this problem himself. After he fed the five thousand, the crowd came looking for him again, and he told them plainly that they were seeking him because they ate their fill of the loaves (John 6:26). He would not become a free table. He said, Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you (John 6:27); and when they asked what work God required, he answered that they should believe in him whom God had sent (John 6:29). The one bread that costs us nothing is Christ himself, and it was paid for at the cross. Every other loaf is to be earned, or given in love to those who cannot earn it.

Not a verse against the poor. The distinction between unwilling and unable is not a modern softening; it is what the verse says. This is the man who organised a major international collection for the poor of Jerusalem across several years and several letters (Romans 15:25–27; 2 Corinthians 8–9), who was eager to remember the poor (Galatians 2:10), who told the Galatians to do good to everyone (Galatians 6:10), and who wrote that anyone who does not provide for his household has denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8). A verse used to justify indifference to the poor is being used against its author. Early churches shared meals and supported the needy generously (Acts 2:44–45; 4:34–35), and that generosity could be exploited; the rule protects the church’s charity for those who truly need it. It is a rule for the community’s table, not by itself a settlement of every question of public welfare policy. Refusing to subsidise a choice is a different act from abandoning a person, and v. 15 will make sure nobody confuses them. Nor does a person’s worth depend on productivity; every human bears God’s image, and the one who finds his whole worth in his job has made the opposite mistake to the idle. Underneath it, idleness is a failure of love (1 Thessalonians 4:11–12): the idle man’s food comes from somewhere, and the somewhere is his brothers. The command is not an attack on the poor. It is a defence of them.

How do I apply this when someone asks me for money? Begin with generosity, not suspicion: give to the one who begs from you (Matthew 5:42) is still Christ’s word. But generosity can be wise. Where you can, give in ways that meet real needs, food, a bill paid directly, help finding work, rather than cash that may feed an addiction. Within the church, let the deacons or leaders who know the situation guide the help, so that the genuinely needy are cared for generously and the able but unwilling are lovingly pressed to work. When in doubt, err on the side of mercy, and ask God for wisdom (James 1:5).

On a Tuesday. Do today’s work as to the Lord (Colossians 3:23), who gives the strength for it. If you are tempted to coast, remember that someone is carrying what you put down. And when you have coasted, as we all do, remember that Christ’s work never faltered and is counted as yours (Romans 5:19); return to your own in gratitude, not dread.

verseByVerse.quote: For we hear that some among you walk in idleness, not busy at work, but busybodies. Now such persons we command and encourage in the Lord Jesus Christ to do their work quietly and to earn their own living.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some among you. Paul had received a report, perhaps from the bearer of the first letter. “Some” (tinas): not the whole church, but a group, living the disorderly life of v. 6.

Not busy at work, but busybodies. The English catches a pun that is in the Greek too: mēden ergazomenous alla periergazomenous, not working, but working around. Doing no business, but minding everyone else’s. The wordplay is the diagnosis. Idleness is never actually idle. The energy does not disappear when a person stops working; it gets redirected into other people’s affairs: spreading gossip, interfering, perhaps stirring up excitement about the end. Idleness and meddling go together (1 Timothy 5:13), and in a small community the meddling does real damage, which is why this is a church problem and not a private one. Underneath, meddling often feeds a quieter hunger: to matter, to be in the know, to manage other people’s lives when one’s own has been left unmanaged. The first letter had already told them to mind their own affairs (1 Thessalonians 4:11). The advice had not taken.

Command and encourage. Paul speaks directly to the idle, with two verbs: the command, and parakaleō, urge, appeal, the coming-alongside word. He does not choose between firmness and warmth. “In the Lord Jesus Christ”: both the authority and the motive are Christ. Paul does not write them off; he calls them back.

Quietly. The phrase (meta hēsychias) means with calmness: the opposite of the restless, meddling busyness of v. 11. It echoes 1 Thessalonians 4:11: aspire to live quietly, mind your own affairs, and work with your hands. Quietness here is not silence but a settled, undisturbed way of life. The cure for meddling is not a rule against gossip; it is a job.

Their own living. Literally, that they eat their own bread: a direct echo of v. 8, where Paul did not eat anyone’s bread without paying. He is asking them to do exactly what he did in front of them. Self-support frees a person to be generous to others: let him labour, doing honest work with his own hands, so that he may have something to share with anyone in need (Ephesians 4:28).

What it does not mean. It does not mean every Christian must be in paid employment. Homemaking, caring for family, study and volunteer service are real work. The issue is refusing responsibility and living off others while meddling in their affairs.

Is retirement unbiblical? Not if it is a change of work rather than an end to usefulness. Scripture nowhere commands paid employment to the end of life, and age and weakness are real. But it gives no picture of a long life of self-pleasing leisure either. Retirement can free a believer for prayer, for grandchildren, for serving the church, for hospitality, for mentoring younger Christians, for volunteer work in the community (Titus 2:3–5; Psalm 92:14). The question is not whether you draw a salary, but whether your time is given to God and others or simply spent on yourself.

On a Tuesday. Before you pass on the next piece of news about someone, ask: is this mine to tell, and have I finished what God gave me to do today?
verseByVerse.note: A wordplay in Greek: not busy at work (ergazomenous) but busybodies (periergazomenous).

verseByVerse.quote: As for you, brothers, do not grow weary in doing good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for you, brothers. The phrase (hymeis de, but you) turns from the idle to the rest of the church, the faithful majority who were working and perhaps supporting the idle.

Do not grow weary. The verb (enkakēsēte) means lose heart, give up from exhaustion. “Doing good” (kalopoiountes) is a single compound word: doing what is fine, noble, right. There is a second casualty in this situation: the people who have been working all along, paying their own way, carrying more than their share, and watching others eat at the common table without contributing. When disorder is tolerated, the orderly begin to wonder why they bother. The steady giver notices who is not giving; the reliable one starts to feel like a fool. That corrosion can do more long-term damage than the original idleness, because it works on the people holding everything up.

A hand on the shoulder. Paul does not tell the faithful to police the others or to keep accounts. To everyone else he simply says: keep going. Refusing to enable idleness is itself doing good; what he guards against is a swing from naive generosity to cold suspicion. “Doing good” covers the whole of generous, useful Christian living, so the verse reaches past Thessalonica to anyone who has been faithful for a long time without much to show for it, and who has begun to calculate. The same exhortation appears in Galatians 6:9, with the promise that in due season we will reap, if we do not give up.

Consider him. The New Testament’s answer to weariness in well-doing is a Person. Consider him who endured from sinners such hostility against himself, says Hebrews, so that you may not grow weary or fainthearted (Hebrews 12:3). The Lord Jesus healed lepers who never came back to thank him, fed crowds who wanted only bread, and washed the feet of the man who would betray him. His goodness was not withdrawn when it was abused, and we ourselves, who took far more than we gave, are the proof.

I am exhausted from serving. Does this mean I can never rest? No. Growing weary in doing good means losing heart and giving up, not needing sleep or a holiday. God built rest into creation, and Jesus took his tired disciples away to rest a while (Mark 6:31). Sometimes the faithful thing is to step back from a role for a season, to share the load, or to say no to a new request. What Paul warns against is the bitterness that says: no one appreciates this, so I will stop caring. Rest your body; guard your heart. And remember that the harvest is promised, even when you cannot see it yet.

On a Tuesday. Think of one good thing you used to do and quietly stopped doing because someone took advantage, or because no one noticed. Ask whether God wants you to begin again, more wisely.

For worship. No kindness done in the name of the Lord Jesus is lost. He counts it as done to himself: the meal given, the visit made, the help quietly offered to a brother who never said thank you. As you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, he will say, you did it to me (Matthew 25:40). He sees what no one else noticed, and one day he will thank his servants himself.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone does not obey what we say in this letter, take note of that person, and have nothing to do with him, that he may be ashamed. Do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What we say in this letter. Here is the procedure. Paul’s written word carries the same authority as his spoken word (2:15). Refusing it is refusing apostolic authority, and that bears on how we treat the New Testament today: it is the apostles’ word to the church, and it binds us.

Take note of that person. The verb (sēmeiousthe) means mark, identify. The church is to recognise openly who is persisting in disobedience, rather than letting everyone gossip about it privately.

Have nothing to do with him. The phrase (mē synanamignysthai) means do not mix together with. It is the same rare word as 1 Corinthians 5:9, 11, and the same withdrawal as v. 6: the removal of the ordinary fellowship and support that had made the behaviour sustainable. It likely means withdrawing table fellowship and close social intimacy, possibly including the Lord’s Supper, so that the person feels the break.

That he may be ashamed. The verb (entrapē) describes a man brought up short, who suddenly sees how his behaviour looks. Paul is not after humiliation for its own sake. In a community where a person genuinely belongs, that recognition is a mercy, because it is the thing that changes him. The aim is repentance, an outcome for him, not protection for everyone else.

Warn him as a brother. “Warn” (noutheteite) means admonish, set a person’s mind right: correction aimed at change, not at punishment. Discipline is family correction, not the expulsion of an enemy. So the withdrawal is real and it is limited. The community stops subsidising and stops pretending nothing is wrong; it does not stop speaking to him, and it does not reclassify him as an opponent. Everything in the procedure is designed to get him back.

Where Christians differ: is this the same as excommunication? Some see this as full exclusion from the church; others as a lesser stage. Verdict: This seems to be a step short of full excommunication. In Matthew 18:17 and 1 Corinthians 5:5, 13, the unrepentant is put outside and treated as an unbeliever. Here the offender is still to be warned “as a brother.” Discipline has stages: private warning, warning with witnesses, the church’s withdrawal of close fellowship, and, if repentance never comes, removal from membership. At every stage the goal is restoration (2 Corinthians 2:6–8; Galatians 6:1).

The narrow line. A church that cannot hold both halves will fail in one of two directions, and both are common. Drop the firmness and you get a congregation that tolerates anything and therefore helps nobody: the person is left exactly as he is, which is not kindness. Drop the warmth and discipline becomes expulsion: an enemy made, a person written off, and no road home. Paul walks the narrow line between them in two sentences. Behind both halves stands the holiness of the Lord whose name the church bears: a church that shrugs at sin misrepresents him as surely as a church that forgets his mercy.

Not an enemy. The church may not treat the disobedient brother as an enemy because of how it was treated itself. While we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (Romans 5:10), and the Son is not ashamed to call those he saves his brothers (Hebrews 2:11). A congregation of former enemies made family by Christ cannot write off a brother without forgetting how it got there. And Christ’s own way with a failing disciple set the pattern. He warned Peter plainly, let him feel the weight of his denial, and then went after him by the lake with the question, Do you love me? (John 21:15–17). Firm, personal and aimed entirely at restoration: that is discipline in his name.

What it does not mean. It does not license harshness, public shaming for entertainment, or cutting off all contact. Nor does it mean individuals should begin discipline on their own; it is the church’s act, led by its elders.

What do I do if someone under church discipline is my friend? Stay a friend in the way Paul describes: not by pretending nothing has happened, and not by taking his side against the church, but by being one of the voices that calls him back. Do not gossip about the matter, and do not join in easy socialising that tells him all is well. Do speak to him, pray for him, and tell him plainly that you want him restored. If you think the church has acted wrongly, raise it with the elders, not with him. And be ready to be the first to welcome him when he repents (2 Corinthians 2:7–8).

On a Tuesday. If you must correct a fellow believer, settle in your heart before you speak that you want him back more than you want to be proved right. And if you are the one being corrected, receive it as a brother’s warning, not an enemy’s attack.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peace, a signature, and grace: the letter closes with a blessing that includes every member of the church (vv. 16–18).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord of Peace, and a Signature Against Forgery

Only here does Paul write ‘the Lord of peace’, saying of Christ what a Jew would say of God; and his handwritten signature (v. 17) answers the forged letter of 2:2 with a test the church can actually use.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: To a year-old, harassed congregation Paul wrote of flaming fire and the son of destruction, and signed off with grace.

Now: ‘All’, twice in three verses (vv. 16, 18), puts even the disciplined inside the blessing.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may the Lord of peace himself give you peace at all times in every way. The Lord be with you all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord of peace himself. Elsewhere Paul writes the God of peace (1 Thessalonians 5:23; Romans 15:33). Here, uniquely in his letters, it is the Lord of peace, and Lord in these letters usually means Jesus: Christ, who is the source and giver of peace (John 14:27; Ephesians 2:14). It is another of the unargued places where Paul says of Christ what a Jew would only say of God. “Himself” is emphatic, as at 2:16: peace comes directly from him, not from circumstances, not from a technique for calming down. Peace here is not a state they must achieve but a gift that has to be handed over.

At all times in every way. “Peace” (eirēnē, Hebrew shalom) is not only calm feelings, but wholeness, well-being, and right relationship with God and one another. Then two phrases that leave nothing out. At all times: no moment excluded, including the ones in which the trouble is at its worst. And in every way: in every form, or by every means, however it has to be delivered. Some manuscripts read in every place. This church had persecution from outside, false teaching within and disorder at the common table, and Paul is not describing the absence of trouble; there is no prospect of that. He is asking for something to be given in the middle of it (John 16:33).

The Lord be with you all. One of the oldest and simplest blessings there is (Ruth 2:4). The greatest blessing is the Lord’s presence: I am with you always, to the end of the age (Matthew 28:20). And note the last word. You all: which in this congregation must include the idle brothers of v. 6 and whoever was to be marked in v. 14. Paul has just told the church to withdraw from them, and he will not close the letter without including them in the blessing. That is the difference between discipline and rejection, said in one word.

How do I actually receive this peace? By receiving the Lord who gives it. Peace is not a technique but a Person: he himself is our peace (Ephesians 2:14). Begin with the peace with God that comes through faith in Christ (Romans 5:1), which no circumstance can disturb. Then bring each anxiety to him in prayer with thanksgiving, and his peace will guard your heart (Philippians 4:6–7). Fix your mind on what is true about him (Isaiah 26:3). And do not wait for the trouble to end before expecting peace; Paul prayed for it at all times, which includes now.

For worship. The Lord of peace made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). He calmed the storm with a word and slept through it first. He walked into a locked room full of frightened men and said, peace be with you, and showed them his hands. That same Lord is with you all, the faithful and the faltering, and his peace is not a mood that comes and goes but the gift of his own presence, which never leaves.

verseByVerse.quote: I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. This is the sign of genuineness in every letter of mine; it is the way I write.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With my own hand. The handwriting changes on the page. Paul normally dictated his letters to a secretary (an amanuensis; compare Romans 16:22, where Tertius names himself) and then took the pen for the last lines (1 Corinthians 16:21; Galatians 6:11; Colossians 4:18). His handwriting was evidently distinctive: see with what large letters I am writing to you with my own hand (Galatians 6:11).

The sign of genuineness. “Sign” (sēmeion) means mark, token. This time there is a reason beyond affection. Go back to 2:2, where the trouble started: they had been shaken by a letter seeming to be from us. His handwritten signature lets them tell his true letters from forgeries, and it authenticates the whole letter, not only the lines he signed. “In every letter” implies Paul had already written others, or intended this as his regular practice, and that the church would keep and compare his letters. Writing very early, Paul already expects his letters to circulate, and knows they carry weight worth counterfeiting.

It is the way I write. Literally, thus I write. He answers a forged letter not only with argument, which he has already given them in chapter 2, but with a procedure they can actually use next time. Pastors who have only theology and no practical remedies leave their people defenceless in the interval. The written half of the deposit of 2:15 had to be protected, and here is Paul protecting it in the only way available to him: with his own hand at the bottom of the page.

Whose voice is protected. Paul guards his signature so carefully because of whose authority it carries. He was an apostle not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father (Galatians 1:1). To forge Paul’s letter was to put words in the mouth of the risen Lord who sent him, and to read his genuine letter is to hear that Lord, who had promised that the Spirit would bring to the apostles’ remembrance all that he had said to them (John 14:26). The hand at the foot of the page is Paul’s, but the voice it protects is Christ’s, and that is why the church has always cared which letters are genuine.

Textual note. Some critical scholars argue that 2 Thessalonians was not written by Paul, partly because of its strong stress on authenticity, claiming a forger would protest too much. But the stress fits the situation exactly: a forged letter had already caused trouble (2:2). Others point to differences of tone and end-time teaching from 1 Thessalonians, though a changed situation explains them well. The early church received the letter as Paul’s without dispute; it is listed in Marcion’s canon and the Muratorian Fragment, probably echoed by Polycarp and quoted by Irenaeus. The case against Paul is far from compelling, and this commentary receives the letter as his.

How do we know the books in our Bible are genuine and not forgeries? The same way the Thessalonians did, extended over time. The early churches received the apostles’ letters directly, kept them, copied them and compared them, and they rejected writings that falsely claimed apostolic authority. The books of the New Testament were recognised, not invented, by the church: they carried apostolic origin, agreed with the apostolic gospel, and were received from the beginning by the churches. Above all, God’s word bears its own marks, and the Spirit persuades his people that it is his voice (the Westminster Confession 1.5; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.5; John 10:27). The canon is closed: no new writing can join it, and none needs to.

On a Tuesday. When a book, a video or a preacher claims to tell you something new from God, ask the Thessalonian question: where is the apostle’s signature on this? If it is not in Scripture, it does not bind your conscience.
verseByVerse.note: Paul dictated his letters, then signed off in his own hand — a safeguard against forgeries such as the one hinted at in 2:2.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. “Grace” (charis) is undeserved favour and its gifts. Paul began with grace (1:2) and ends with grace, as he framed the first letter (1 Thessalonians 1:1; 5:28). Everything in this letter, comfort in persecution, the panic about the day of the Lord, the man of lawlessness, the busybodies, discipline, sits inside its opening and closing grace. It comes to us from him and through him, the crucified and risen Lord.

Be with you all. The same as 1 Thessalonians 5:28, but with all added, as in v. 16: the final sentence of the letter puts even those just marked for discipline inside the blessing. Grace is for the whole church, including the disorderly, whom grace alone can restore.

The note it ends on. Nothing in these three chapters, not the flaming fire, not the eternal ruin, not the withdrawal of fellowship, has been written out of hostility toward anybody. It has been written to hold a church together under pressure and to get its wandering members back. Remember what this congregation was: former pagans and God-fearers from the synagogue in a proud Roman city (Acts 17:4; 1 Thessalonians 1:9), the church perhaps a year or so old, harassed, confused and quarrelling about who should be working. To such people he wrote about flaming fire and the son of destruction and the glory of the Lord Jesus, and then signed off with the only thing that was going to get them through the week. Grace, to the whole lot of them, because nothing else would last.

What it does not mean. It does not mean grace ignores sin. The same letter disciplines sin. Grace both forgives and transforms: the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation, training us to renounce ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12).

On a Tuesday. End the day where Paul ended the letter. Whatever went wrong, whatever you failed to do, whatever you still fear about tomorrow, place it inside the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and pray that same grace, by name, over the person in your church you find hardest to love.

For worship. Grace found the Thessalonians in their idols and kept them under persecution; grace answered their panic, corrected their disorder and promised them glory. It is the grace of a Lord who will come in flaming fire to be glorified in his saints, and who first came in weakness to be crucified for them. To him who gives it freely, and who will come again to complete it, be glory for ever.
